papers.title: Sleep Regularity in Young Adults With and Without Unmanaged Sleep Disorders.
papers.abstract: Irregular sleep is associated with negative health and performance outcomes, including cardiovascular disease and impaired attentional performance. Young adults with unmanaged sleep disorders may be particularly vulnerable to health and safety risks associated with irregular sleep, but sleep regularity in this group is not yet well-characterized. This study describes sleep regularity in young adults with unmanaged sleep disorders relative to healthy sleepers. Seventy-two young adults (60% female; Age [mean ± SD] = 25.1 ± 4.6 years) recorded sleep-wake patterns using daily diaries over 7-21 days. Sleep disorder diagnoses were confirmed by trained clinicians using the Structured Clinical Interview for Sleep Disorders (Revised; SCISD-R), diagnostic polysomnography and validated questionnaires (e.g., Insomnia Severity Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale). Sleep regularity was quantified using the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI). Bootstrapped regressions were used to compare SRI between sleep disorder types and healthy sleepers. Of the sleep disorder groups examined, only individuals with Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (DSWPD) exhibited significantly lower SRI (Median SRI (IQR): 75.8(66.6-80.7)) than healthy sleepers (79.4(76.0-85.0)), B = -8.4, 95% CI[-15.5, -2.1]. There was a trend towards lower SRI in individuals presenting with DSWPD comorbid with Obstructive Sleep Apnea (72.2(66.0-78.2)), B = -10.5[-25.0, 2.1]; and Insomnia (78.2(69.7-81.1)), B = -3.6[-8.9 to 2.0]. Lower sleep regularity in young adults with DSWPD likely reflects a misalignment between biological sleep timing and external obligations (e.g., early morning commitments). Regularizing sleep-wake timing may be a worthwhile target in DSWPD treatment. Further research is warranted to consider the effect of targeted sleep regularity interventions in this population alongside existing treatment recommendations. Trial Registration: Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12624000339550.

papers.title: Automated Home-Cage Sipper Devices Reveal Age and Sex Differences in Ethanol Consumption Patterns.
papers.abstract: Alcohol consumption and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are influenced by circadian rhythms, which differ with age and sex. Little research has compared circadian ethanol consumption patterns across ages and sexes. Cost-effective, open-source Arduino-based home-cage sipper devices could elucidate these patterns. We hypothesized these devices would reveal phase and/or amplitude changes in circadian drinking rhythms in ethanol-drinking mice that would vary by age and sex. We used Arduino-based home-cage sipper devices in continuous-access two-bottle choice (2 bc) with water and ethanol (10% v/v) for 14 days to measure drinking patterns of male and female adolescent (3-week), young adult (6-week), and mature adult (18-week) C57BL/6J mice. Grams per kilogram (g/kg) fluid consumption was manually recorded at the beginning of each dark cycle, while sipper devices continuously recorded drinking. Manually collected 2 bc data confirmed greater ethanol consumption in females and stepwise decreases in total fluid consumption with age in ethanol-drinking females and in both sexes in the water-only groups. Correlations of manually recorded versus sipper count data were strong and significant for ethanol, but weaker for water. Blood ethanol concentrations significantly correlated with sipper data, indicating sipper devices can determine temporal ethanol consumption. Sipper devices uncovered subtle differences in circadian rhythms by age, group, and ethanol consumption, including minor phase advancement with ethanol consumption with age in females, but delay in males, as well as a female-specific phase delay and weaker amplitude in total fluid consumption across age groups with ethanol consumption. We show these devices capture circadian patterns of drinking behavior differing by age, sex, and ethanol consumption inaccessible by manual 2 bc measurements. Future studies may examine older age groups and further dissect circadian drinking patterns by age and sex and their molecular mechanisms relevant to AUD pathogenesis.

papers.title: Association of Dietary Quality and Working Hours With Sleep Health in US Adults: Evidence From National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2007-2014.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess the respective associations of dietary quality and working hours with insufficient sleep and sleep disorders among US adults and to examine the associations of combined work-diet patterns. In this cross-sectional study, data were obtained from the 2007-2014 NHANES. Dietary quality was assessed using the Healthy Eating Index 2015 (HEI-2015), and working hours were measured based on self-reported weekly working hours. Four work-diet patterns were created according to dietary quality and working hours. Insufficient sleep was defined as a sleep duration of ≤ 6 h, and sleep disorders were self-reported by respondents. Weighted logistic regression was used as the primary analysis. Among the 8339 respondents, 41.1% experienced insufficient sleep and 6.9% reported sleep disorders. In the fully adjusted model, higher dietary quality was not significantly associated with insufficient sleep (OR: 0.834, 95% CI: 0.693-1.005) or sleep disorders (OR: 0.716, 95% CI: 0.506-1.014). Shorter working hours were associated with lower odds of insufficient sleep (OR: 0.828, 95% CI: 0.720-0.952), but not sleep disorders (OR: 0.848, 95% CI: 0.661-1.088). Regarding the combined work-diet patterns, individuals with a healthy diet and shorter working hours had significantly lower odds of insufficient sleep (OR: 0.697, 95% CI: 0.568-0.854) and sleep disorders (OR: 0.623, 95% CI: 0.439-0.882) after adjustment for potential confounders. In this nationally representative study, a healthy diet and shorter working hours were associated with lower odds of insufficient sleep and sleep disorders. Maintaining healthy dietary habits together with reasonable working hours may be associated with better sleep health.

papers.title: Implementing a Comprehensive Patient-Reported Outcome Framework for Chronic Urticaria in Clinical Practice.
papers.abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a burdensome inflammatory skin condition that substantially impairs health-related quality of life and is frequently accompanied by sleep disturbances and psychiatric comorbidities such as anxiety and depression. While international guidelines advocate continuous assessment with patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), clinical inertia and time constraints limit their real-world implementation. To propose a practical, two-level framework that guides integrating PROMs into routine clinical practice. Narrative review informed by the expertise of members of Urticaria Centers of Reference and Excellence (UCARE), based on searches of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus (last 10 years) and the 2026 international guideline. The core set, applied to all patients with CSU at every visit, comprises the UAS7 (disease activity), the UCT (disease control) and the CU-Q2oL (quality of life). Second-level assessments are added according to clinical need: angioedema-specific instruments (AAS, AECT, AE-QoL), instruments for chronic inducible urticarias, and brief screening tools for mental health and sleep (e.g., PHQ-4, PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI) in patients with poorly controlled disease, high quality-of-life impact or a suggestive history. Digital platforms such as the CRUSE application can support data collection alongside paper diaries. This framework may help clinicians detect uncontrolled disease and often overlooked comorbidities and align management with international guidelines. Its feasibility and impact require prospective evaluation.

papers.title: How Perceived Traits Modulate the Neural Processing of Reward During Reinforcement Learning.
papers.abstract: Humans infer others' traits through positive and negative feedback, and these perceived traits, in turn, shape how individuals perceive others' behavior. Although previous studies have investigated the neural basis of reward and trait learning, the temporal dynamics by which trait-level learning signals modulate reward-related brain responses during learning remain poorly understood. In this study, we used reinforcement learning models to separate participants' processing of reward and generosity prediction errors (PEs), and used EEG to examine how perceived traits modulate the neural processing of reward. Behavioral analyses indicated that both reward and perceived generosity influenced decision making during the learning phase. In the test phase, perceived trait information played a more significant role in guiding decisions. Neurally, positive reward PEs elicited larger reward positivity amplitudes, stronger delta power, and reduced N400 amplitudes compared to negative reward PEs only when generosity PEs were negative. This pattern may reflect an increased focus on reward outcomes when experienced generosity is less than expected during the learning phase. These results elucidate how trait learning asymmetrically modulates reward salience and evaluation, a mechanism that may promote the prioritization of social knowledge in future choices.

papers.title: Treadmill Walking Differentially Modulates Early Auditory Responses to Standard and Deviant Sounds.
papers.abstract: People often encounter environmental sounds while walking without attending to them, but it is unclear whether walking alters early cortical responses to these sounds. We recorded 32-channel electroencephalography from 22 healthy young adults during a passive auditory frequency-oddball paradigm. Conditions were sitting and treadmill walking without an object, with a water-filled cup or with a clay-filled cup matched for mass and apparent fill height. The four conditions were compared in two pairs: sitting versus walking without carrying, and water versus clay carrying. In each comparison, we examined standard- and deviant-evoked responses in the N1 window and amplitude in the mismatch-negativity window. The sitting versus walking-without-carrying comparison showed a significant stimulus-type by movement-condition interaction 80-130 ms after sound onset. In separate, unadjusted comparisons of sitting and walking for each stimulus type, the deviant-evoked response was attenuated during walking, whereas the standard-evoked response did not differ significantly between conditions. Sensitivity analyses in the same participants yielded a smaller interaction estimate with the lowest high-pass cutoff, but filter-setting differences were unclear. In the comparison of water and clay carrying, the conditions differed kinematically, but no additional modulation of the measured auditory responses was detected. The comparison of sitting and treadmill walking showed that walking-related changes in early auditory responses differed between standard and deviant sounds. However, the contributions of frequency, probability and adaptation to this response difference could not be separated.

papers.title: Twenty-One Years of Bariatric Surgery in Benin Republic: Evolution of Techniques and Outcomes.
papers.abstract: Bariatric surgery was introduced in the Republic of Benin in 2005, yet, as in many sub-Saharan African countries, it has remained almost entirely undocumented. To describe how bariatric surgical techniques and their outcomes have evolved in Benin over a 21-year-period. Retrospective cohort study including all patients who underwent bariatric surgery between January 1, 2005, and January 31, 2026, at two hospitals in Cotonou, Benin. A total of 111 patients were included (mean age, 43.3 years; women, 85.6%; mean body mass index, 43.2 kg/m2). The procedures performed were laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (50.5%), adjustable gastric banding (37.8%), open sleeve gastrectomy (10.8%), and gastric bipartition (.9%). Gastric banding was discontinued in 2011, and laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy has been the standard procedure since 2012. Excess weight loss at 48 months was 50% after sleeve gastrectomy versus 21% after gastric banding. At 48 months, sleep apnea, hypertension, and diabetes persisted in 8%, 11%, and 12% of patients after sleeve gastrectomy, compared with 35%, 36%, and 40% after gastric banding. Morbidity and mortality rates were 6.3% and 1.8%, respectively. Bariatric surgery in Benin has successfully shifted to a minimally invasive approach, but its volume remains very low.
papers.journal: Journal of laparoendoscopic & advanced surgical techniques. Part A

papers.title: A Network Analysis of Sleep-Related Concerns, Insomnia, and Depressive Symptoms Among Shift-Working Nurses.
papers.abstract: Shift-working nurses are vulnerable to sleep-related concerns, insomnia, and depressive symptoms, yet their symptom-level interrelationships remain unclear. This study used network analysis to examine the structure of these symptoms and identify core and bridge symptoms as potential intervention targets. We sought to map the symptom network linking sleep-related concerns, insomnia, and depression in shift-working nurses, and identify central and bridge symptoms. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 703 shift-working registered nurses from a tertiary hospital in Guangzhou, China, in September 2025. Sleep-related concerns, insomnia, and depressive symptoms were assessed using the Anxiety and Preoccupation about Sleep Questionnaire, Athens Insomnia Scale, and Patient Health Questionnaire-9. A regularized Gaussian graphical model was estimated to examine symptom associations. Central and bridge symptoms were identified, and network stability was evaluated using bootstrapping and sensitivity analysis. Insomnia and depressive symptoms were identified in 39.3% and 37.1% of participants, respectively. The symptom network was highly interconnected, with stronger within-cluster than between-cluster associations. Fatigue, worries about sleep problems, and long-term worry about sleep emerged as the most central symptoms. Sleep, daytime mood, and bedtime were the main bridge symptoms linking sleep-related concerns, insomnia, and depressive symptoms. Bootstrap and sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the findings. Sleep-related concerns, insomnia, and depressive symptoms were closely interconnected among shift-working nurses. The identified central and bridge symptoms may inform symptom-focused screening and the development of integrated sleep and mental health interventions for this population, with broader implications for nursing practice and occupational health management.

papers.title: Different Facial EMG and Emotional Expressivity Responses to Insomnia-Related and Sadness-Related Video Clips in People With Insomnia Disorder Compared to Healthy Sleepers With and Without Sleep Restriction.
papers.abstract: Research into emotional processes in insomnia disorder is growing, yet more studies are needed on patients' emotional functioning. This study investigates emotional responses of individuals with insomnia disorder and healthy controls to dynamic emotional stimuli related and unrelated to insomnia. The assessment incorporates physiological, subjective, and behavioural measures of emotional reactivity. The study involved 97 patients with insomnia disorder, 49 healthy controls under moderate sleep restriction, and 47 healthy controls without sleep restriction. In a controlled laboratory setting, participants watched an insomnia-related and a sadness-related video clip. Emotional reactivity was assessed through facial electromyography (EMG), self-report, and coding of video-recorded facial expressions. The spontaneous use of emotion regulation strategies was also assessed. The emotional responses to the two video clips in the three groups were compared in multiple MANCOVAs with emotion-related assessments as dependent variables. EMG revealed a distinct pattern in insomnia patients, showing higher zygomatic and lower corrugator muscle activity during the insomnia-related compared to the sadness-related video clip. Only patients with insomnia disorder reported a pre-to-post video clip increase in arousal in response to the insomnia-related clip. The findings indicate a unique engagement of patients with insomnia when processing emotional stimuli related to their condition. More research using multi-method approaches is needed to differentiate the effect of sleep restriction from that of chronic insomnia disorder. Strategies aimed at addressing emotional processes may prove beneficial in modulating emotional responses to symptoms-related stimuli.

papers.title: Gender Differences of Weight Self-Stigma Among Children Aged 7-12 Years.
papers.abstract: Individuals with excess weight usually experience weight-related stigma. This study aimed to assess gender differences in weight self-stigma (WSS) among children. A cross-sectional survey was conducted between May and July 2023 in five primary schools with convenient sampling in Linhai, China. All students in Grades 1 to 6 were included except for those with somatic or mental disorders. The Weight Self-stigma Questionnaire was used to measure students' WSS. Of the 2619 participants, 1415 (54.0%) were boys and 1204 (46.0%) were girls. The mean age was 10.6 ± 1.0 years for boys and 10.7 ± 0.9 years for girls. The mean BMI was 20.6 ± 6.4 kg/m2 for boys and 19.6 ± 6.1 kg/m2 for girls. WSS scores were higher in boys than in girls (21.9 ± 9.2 versus [vs.] 21.0 ± 9.1; p = 0.012). They were lower in boys with overweight compared to girls (24.7 ± 8.9 vs. 27.0 ± 9.4; p = 0.015). Logistic regression models revealed that overweight (odds ratio [OR]: 2.55, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.93-3.38) and obesity (OR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.36-2.37) were associated factors for high WSS scores among boys. Additionally, age (10 vs. 7∼9 years, OR: 1.68, 95% CI: 1.07-2.62), sleep time during school-day (7∼8 h vs. 10 h, OR: 1.93, 95% CI: 1.31-2.84; 9 h vs. 10 h, OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.16-2.02), and lower family socioeconomic status (OR: 1.62, 95% CI: 1.17-2.24) were associated factors in girls. WSS scores were higher among girls with overweight than in boys. Different methods of weight management should be explored according to gender.

papers.title: Comparison of Oral Hygiene-Related Self-Efficacy and Oral Health Behaviors by Current Smoking Status in Adults.
papers.abstract: Smoking may influence oral health through biological, psychological, and behavioral pathways. This study aimed to compare oral hygiene-related self-efficacy and oral health behaviors according to smoking status. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in January 2026 among 100 Korean adults aged ≥19 years. The participants were classified as current smokers (n=46) or non-smokers (n=54). Oral hygiene-related self-efficacy was assessed using the toothbrushing self-efficacy (TB-SE) and interdental hygiene management self-efficacy (IHM-SE) subscales of the Korean version of the Oral Hygiene-Related Self-Efficacy tool. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-test, chi-square test, and Fisher's exact test. TB-SE was significantly lower in current smokers than in current non-smokers (22.33±5.80 vs. 24.67±3.83; Welch's t=-2.34, p=0.022), with a mean difference of -2.34 points (95% confidence interval, -4.33 to -0.35; Hedges' g=-0.48). IHM-SE did not differ significantly between the groups (20.07±6.22 vs. 19.72±7.28; p=0.802). No significant group differences were observed in tooth brushing at least twice daily, tooth brushing before sleep, dental checkups within the past year, or use of oral hygiene aids (all p>0.05). Current smokers had lower situational self-efficacy for tooth brushing than that of current non-smokers, whereas IHM-SE and major self-reported oral health behaviors did not differ significantly between the groups. These findings suggest that oral health interventions for current smokers may benefit from strategies designed to strengthen TB-SE under challenging daily life conditions.

papers.title: An apparently de novo UBE3A missense variant p.(Tyr777Cys) in the HECT domain in a child with an atypical early childhood phenotype suggestive of Angelman syndrome: a case report and focused literature review.
papers.abstract: Angelman syndrome (AS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with loss of maternal UBE3A function in neurons. Interpreting rare UBE3A missense variants can be challenging, particularly when parental origin and functional effects have not been established. We report a 30-month-old Chinese boy with global developmental delay, motor impairment, and severe expressive language impairment, without clinically observed seizures during the available follow-up. Genetic evaluation, including trio whole-exome sequencing and proband whole-genome sequencing, identified an apparently de novo heterozygous UBE3A missense variant, NM_130839.5:c.2330A>G, p. (Tyr777Cys), within the homologous to the E6AP carboxyl terminus (HECT) domain. Copy-number analysis did not identify a large deletion involving 15q11.2-q13. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed paroxysmal high-amplitude 2-3 Hz spike-slow and sharp-slow complexes, and the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) report suggested delayed white-matter myelination. The variant was classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in the laboratory report and remained a VUS following reassessment using the UBE3A-specific ClinGen Variant Curation Expert Panel (VCEP) specifications. Its maternal or paternal allelic origin remains undetermined, and its functional effects have not been experimentally assessed. This report documents the rare, apparently de novo UBE3A HECT-domain variant p. (Tyr777Cys), together with detailed early developmental and electrophysiological findings. Substantial motor and expressive language impairment accompanied by EEG abnormalities suggestive of AS, despite no clinically observed seizures by 30 months, highlights the importance of considering AS during the evaluation of unexplained developmental delay. Integrated clinical assessment, EEG, and family-based genetic testing help identify candidate variants and guide further investigation. Although p. (Tyr777Cys) remains a VUS, the documented phenotype provides a reference for future case comparisons, parent-of-origin studies, and functional investigations.

papers.title: Heterogeneity of Sleep Complaints at Six Sites from 5 to 3,850 m in China: A Latent Class Analysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep complaints are heterogeneous, and classifying workers simply as good or poor sleepers conceals that heterogeneity. We used latent class analysis to identify sleep phenotypes in a multi-site occupational cohort, to describe their demographic and clinical correlates, and to examine whether reported nocturnal oxygen use at the highest site was associated with subjective sleep. A total of 1236 personnel of a single national employer, each posted to one of six worksites in China at altitudes from 5 to 3850 m, completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). Six indicators were entered into a mixed-mode latent class model: five PSQI component scores (subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction) modelled as ordinal, and the standardized ISI total score modelled as continuous. Solutions with one to six classes were compared on the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, the sample-size-adjusted Bayesian information criterion, the bootstrap likelihood ratio test, entropy, smallest class size and interpretability, and were checked by repeated split-half estimation. Indicators not recorded at one site were handled by full-information maximum likelihood. Multinomial logistic regression with site fixed effects identified correlates of class membership. Within the highest site, PSQI and ISI scores were compared between participants who did and did not report nocturnal oxygen use. Four classes were identified: no complaints (34.7%), mild (17.2%), moderate (33.5%) and severe multidimensional sleep disturbance (14.6%), with an entropy of 0.885 and mean posterior probabilities of 0.892 to 0.982. The four-class structure recurred in all ten split-half samples and was unchanged when the sparse sleep-efficiency and hypnotic-use components were added. Modelling the same ordinal indicators as Gaussian, by contrast, produced information criteria that declined at every step without identifying a solution. Having at least one chronic condition was the correlate most consistently associated with the disturbed classes (moderate: adjusted odds ratio 2.48, 95% CI 1.38 to 4.47; severe: 3.49, 95% CI 1.81 to 6.73), and habitual snoring was associated with the severe class (2.00, 95% CI 1.34 to 2.97). Class distribution differed across sites, with the disturbed classes most frequent at the coastal and plain sites. Among participants at 3850 m, those not reporting nocturnal oxygen use scored 0.82 points higher on the PSQI (95% CI 0.16 to 1.48) and 1.17 points higher on the ISI (95% CI 0.16 to 2.18) than those who did; the ISI difference lies below the 6-point change regarded as the minimally important difference for that instrument, and class distribution did not differ by reported use. Four sleep phenotypes graded by severity were identified in this cross-sectional multi-site cohort. In these data, a sleep-efficiency component reconstructed without bedtime and rise time was too sparse to inform classification yet able to generate a spurious class, and fitting a Gaussian mixture to the bounded ordinal components left class enumeration undefined. Chronic illness and habitual snoring accompanied the more disturbed phenotypes. Because the highest-altitude stratum comprises a single site, the site differences reported here cannot be separated from site-specific occupational, demographic and screening characteristics and should not be read as effects of altitude; the nocturnal oxygen comparison is observational and exploratory.

papers.title: Gut Dysbiosis, IL-6, and White Matter Microstructure in Acute mTBI.
papers.abstract: Conventional neuroimaging may show no definite acute abnormalities in mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), although patients can still have post-concussion symptoms, sleep and emotional burden, cognitive changes, and white matter microstructural abnormalities. This study evaluated gut microbiota, systemic inflammation, white matter microstructure, and neuropsychological performance in acute mTBI, and explored associations among key taxa, inflammatory factors, and symptom burden. Twenty-six patients with acute mTBI and 43 matched healthy controls underwent neuropsychological assessment, serum biomarker testing, fecal 16S rRNA sequencing, and diffusion tensor imaging in a cross-sectional analysis of a prospectively enrolled case-control cohort. Tract-based spatial statistics compared fractional anisotropy, radial diffusivity, mean diffusivity, and axial diffusivity with adjustment for age, sex, and years of education. Serum biomarkers and genus-level microbiota comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure, and Spearman correlations assessed microbiota-inflammation-symptom associations. Compared with controls, patients with mTBI had higher post-concussion symptom, PCL-C, BDI, and ISI scores and lower Digit Span-backward scores in unadjusted comparisons. Covariate-adjusted TBSS showed increased radial diffusivity and decreased fractional anisotropy in multiple white matter regions, whereas mean and axial diffusivity did not differ. Serum IL-6 was elevated after FDR correction (q = 0.003), while IL-1β and UCH-L1 were higher only in unadjusted analyses. FDR-adjusted genus-level differences included enrichment of Escherichia-Shigella (q = 0.0333) and depletion of Faecalibacterium (q = 0.0163). Escherichia-Shigella abundance correlated positively with IL-6 (r = 0.812, P < 0.001), and IL-6 correlated with post-concussion symptoms (r = 0.446, P = 0.022); these correlations were exploratory and unadjusted for multiple comparisons. Acute mTBI was associated with covariate-adjusted white matter microstructural abnormalities, FDR-supported IL-6 elevation, and FDR-adjusted gut microbial alterations. The observed microbiota-inflammation-symptom correlations remain exploratory, and their causal and prognostic significance requires longitudinal validation.

papers.title: Beyond decibels alone: environmental noise, auditory diversity, and person-environment interactions in autism.
papers.abstract: Environmental noise is a ubiquitous physical exposure and a biologically active non-auditory stressor, yet its relevance to autism has received substantially less attention compared to chemical components of the urban exposome. Two questions are often conflated: whether prenatal or early-life noise contributes to autism-related neurodevelopmental susceptibility and whether adverse auditory environments increase functional burden after autistic characteristics are present. In this structured narrative review, we integrate environmental epidemiology, developmental and auditory neuroscience, sleep and stress research, and environmental acoustics within a two-pathway life-course framework. PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception through 4 September 2026, supplemented by targeted Google Scholar searching. We included English-language peer-reviewed primary studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and authoritative guidance or standards documents and excluded conference abstracts, dissertations, and preprints. Evidence was prioritized by directness to the autism question, study design, exposure characterization, outcome validity, precision, and recency; the evidence matrix is intentionally selective. Direct human evidence that quantified environmental noise independently increasing the risk of autism diagnosis or persistently worsening autistic traits is sparse and inconsistent, and current data do not support a causal claim. A more direct functional evidence stream-studies conducted on autistic participants that experimentally manipulate auditory conditions and/or measure real-world functional outcomes-indicates that some autistic individuals show altered auditory responsivity, reduced or delayed habituation, speech-in-noise and selective-attention difficulties, and greater burden in noisy or unpredictable settings. We conceptualize this pathway as a person-environment interaction in which acoustic structure, sensory phenotype, task demand, and predictability or control jointly shape functioning. Standard metrics such as LAeq, Lden, and Lnight remain necessary for comparability and policy and are supplemented, not replaced, by multidimensional characterization. Event peaks and temporal fluctuation receive empirical support from studies on child neurodevelopment, whereas spectral content, reverberation, source multiplicity, predictability, controllability, and personal time-activity patterns remain framework-generated hypotheses requiring direct autism-specific testing. This framework separates etiologic inference from phenotypic modification and identifies testable priorities for early-life research and co-designed acoustic accessibility.

papers.title: Reactive angiomatosis secondary to chronic mechanical pressure: A two-patient case series: A case report.
papers.abstract: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is commonly associated with pressure-related cutaneous complications; however, reactive angiomatosis secondary to chronic CPAP mask use has not previously been reported. We present two 65-year-old men with slowly progressive, asymptomatic facial lesions localized to areas of chronic CPAP mask contact, with histopathologic findings demonstrating reactive vascular remodeling and clinicopathologic correlation supporting reactive angiomatosis, including diffuse dermal angiomatosis in one patient. In both patients, lesion distribution closely corresponded to sites of CPAP mask pressure. These cases expand the spectrum of CPAP-associated cutaneous complications and highlight chronic mechanical pressure and altered local vascular dynamics as a potential mechanism for reactive angiomatosis.

papers.title: Interleukin-6, Rumination, and Anxiety Symptoms in Menopausal Women with Insomnia: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance and anxiety symptoms commonly co-occur during the menopausal transition and postmenopause, yet the biological and cognitive-affective factors associated with anxiety burden remain unclear. This study examined inflammatory and cognitive-affective correlates of anxiety symptoms in menopausal insomnia and investigated whether interleukin-6 (IL-6) and rumination showed parallel indirect associations between sleep-related attributions and anxiety symptoms. A total of 160 women in the menopausal transition or postmenopause were included, comprising 50 healthy controls, 60 women with insomnia but without anxiety symptoms, and 50 women with insomnia and anxiety symptoms. Clinical assessments covered sleep quality, insomnia severity, anxiety symptoms, sleep-related attributions measured by the Sleep Disturbance Questionnaire (SDQ), and rumination measured by the Ruminative Responses Scale (RRS). Serum IL-6 and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured. Group differences in inflammatory markers were examined using covariate-adjusted analyses. Among women with insomnia (n = 110), partial Spearman correlations and bootstrap indirect-effect models were conducted with adjustment for age, education, body mass index, and insomnia duration. Women with insomnia and anxiety symptoms showed the highest IL-6 levels and RRS scores among the three groups. Among women with insomnia, SDQ scores were associated with ln(IL-6), RRS scores, and anxiety symptom scores. In the parallel indirect-effect model, SDQ scores showed a total indirect association with anxiety symptom scores through ln(IL-6) and RRS scores (effect = 0.163, 95% bootstrap CI 0.082-0.264), with specific indirect associations through ln(IL-6) (effect = 0.068, 95% bootstrap CI 0.011-0.151) and RRS scores (effect = 0.096, 95% bootstrap CI 0.037-0.173). The indirect association through ln(CRP) was not supported. Anxiety symptoms in menopausal women with insomnia were associated with sleep-related attributions, IL-6, and rumination. These findings highlight the potential relevance of inflammatory and cognitive-affective factors for understanding anxiety symptom heterogeneity in menopausal women with insomnia.

papers.title: Lifestyle- and health-related challenges in children with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Children with autism spectrum disorder experience a variety of co-occurring health challenges that extend beyond core diagnostic features. Lifestyle-related behaviors, particularly physical activity, dietary patterns, and sleep, are increasingly recognized as closely associated with physical health, behavioral regulation, and overall well-being in this population. However, existing research has largely examined these behaviors in isolation. This systematic review synthesized the evidence published from 2015 to 2025 on physical activity, nutrition, and sleep behaviors in children with ASD, with a specific focus on how these lifestyle domains interact in relation to health and well-being. A thorough and systematic search of three major databases-PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science-was carried out in strict accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Observational, qualitative, and review studies examining lifestyle-related behaviors among children (≤18 years) with ASD were included. Methodological quality was appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, and findings were synthesized narratively. Evidence indicated frequent co-occurrence of lifestyle disruptions associated with cumulative obesity risk, cardiometabolic dysregulation, gastrointestinal symptoms, behavioral and emotional difficulties, reduced functional capacity, and increased caregiver burden. Consistent patterns emerged across studies, including reduced physical activity and elevated sedentary behavior, which were frequently associated with obesity risk, cardiometabolic abnormalities, and behavioral dysregulation, gastrointestinal symptoms, and caregiver burden. Lifestyle-related health behaviors in children with ASD are interconnected and best understood as part of a dynamic system. Integrated, autism-informed approaches addressing physical activity, diet, and sleep concurrently warrant prospective evaluation to determine whether they can support long-term health and well-being.
papers.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

papers.title: Digital Phenotyping of Behavioral Instability as an Early Detection of Clinically Relevant Deterioration in Mental Health: Prospective Observational Multicenter Study.
papers.abstract: Early detection of clinically relevant changes remains a major challenge in mental health, as deterioration unfolds through subtle alterations in daily functioning. Advances in digital phenotyping and smartphone-based monitoring offer new opportunities to capture real-world settings. However, existing approaches rely on active self-reports, and few studies have examined whether within-person instability in passively sensed behavior can anticipate clinically recorded relapse events across diagnoses. This study aimed to adapt and evaluate an algorithm detecting behavioral changes associated with deterioration using passively collected smartphone data from a prospective, multicenter project investigating smartphone-based behavioral monitoring in adults with mental health conditions, to evaluate its performance in-sample and examine whether instability in behavioral patterns can serve as an early marker of relapse. We conducted a prospective, observational, multicenter study including 92 adult participants with mental health conditions (bipolar disorder, personality disorder, substance use disorder, and dual pathology) recruited from 2 specialized mental health centers in Madrid, Spain. Passive behavioral data, including physical activity, mobility, phone use, sleep, and daily routine indicators, were collected using a mobile app over periods ranging from 1 month to 1 year (mean follow-up of 123, SD 94.85 days). Behavioral profiles were generated using heterogeneous mixture models, and changes in behavioral stability were detected using a Bayesian online change-point detection approach. Model hyperparameters and source combinations were selected by grid search and heuristic exploration, and performance was evaluated in-sample by comparing detected change points with relapse events recorded in the electronic health record, using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Forty relapse events with available passive data were included in the analysis. The best-performing model achieved a mean in-sample area under the curve of 82.99% (SD 2.49%). At a false positive rate (FPR) of 5%, the model reached an average true positive rate (TPR) of 40.12% (95% CI 36.61%-43.63%), increasing to 61.10% (95% CI 56.42%-65.79%) at 10% FPR. Model performance was influenced by the temporal aggregation parameter, with optimal results obtained using minimal accumulation of past observations. Multimodal combinations integrating sleep, activity, and routine structure achieved the highest performance. These operating points correspond to decision thresholds matched at the specified FPR values, and the reported intervals reflect variability across 10 stochastic reruns on the same dataset rather than out-of-sample generalization. Performance showed run-to-run variability (maximum TPR of 53.58% vs mean TPR of 40.12%, SD 5.66% at 5% FPR), indicating limited stability. Behavioral instability shows preliminary potential for the early detection of behavioral changes associated with clinically relevant deterioration. Because hyperparameters, source combinations, and thresholds were tuned on the same events used for evaluation, the performance should be interpreted as an in-sample estimate, and external validation is required before clinical application.

papers.title: Shedding Light on Autophagy: Autophagy-Light Signalling Crosstalk Shaping Growth and Metabolism.
papers.abstract: Light is both an energy source and a regulatory signal that shapes plant development, metabolism and environmental acclimation. Autophagy, a conserved degradation and recycling pathway, maintains cellular homoeostasis by reallocating resources and removing damaged components. Although these processes have often been studied separately, emerging evidence reveals that light signalling and autophagy are mechanistically intertwined. In this review, we examine how spectral cues, circadian timing, photodamage and metabolic status converge on autophagy to balance growth with cellular recycling. We highlight transcriptional and epigenetic control of ATG genes, metabolic regulation via the TOR-SnRK1 axis, selective autophagic turnover of light-signalling regulators and organelle quality-control pathways that remove damaged chloroplasts, peroxisomes and mitochondria. We further discuss how this interface contributes to darkness-associated carbon remobilisation, senescence-linked nitrogen recycling, lipophagy and possible connection with specialised metabolism. Finally, we highlight conceptual and technical gaps and propose experimental strategies, including spectral manipulation, autophagy reporters, phosphoproteomics and optogenetic approaches, to dissect the light-autophagy interface. By consolidating these insights, we provide a blueprint for testing how interactions between light signalling and autophagy affect plant stress resilience and metabolic output, and whether they contribute to developmental plasticity.

papers.title: Quality of sleep and fertility quality of life among women undergoing IVF-ET: Mediating role of self-esteem.
papers.abstract: The study aimed to investigate the mediating role of self-esteem in the relationship between quality of sleep and fertility quality of life among women undergoing IVF treatment. The study was conducted among 387 women undergoing IVF in Kerala, using Fertility Quality of Life Questionnaire, Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale and Inventory of Quality of sleep. The results indicated a positive correlation among quality of sleep, self-esteem and quality of life. The findings of the mediation analysis showed that the total effect of quality of sleep on fertility quality of life was significant (β = 0.4392). The direct effect of quality of sleep on fertility quality of life was significant (β = 0.1959). The indirect effect of quality of sleep on fertility quality of life through self-esteem was also statistically significant (β = 0.244). The findings suggest that self-esteem serves as a partial mediator in the relationship between quality of sleep and fertility quality of life for women undergoing IVF.

papers.title: Longitudinal ACC Alterations with Low-Dose Pregabalin in pBMS.
papers.abstract: Primary burning mouth syndrome (pBMS) is a chronic orofacial pain disorder in which the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) serves as a core node in descending pain modulation and central sensitization. Multiparametric MRI evidence for structural, metabolic, and functional abnormalities across ACC subregions remains limited. This single-arm, prospective longitudinal study characterized ACC subregional alterations in 38 patients with moderate-to-severe pBMS and 31 matched healthy controls. All patients received a standardized 4-wk low-dose pregabalin course, with clinical and neuroimaging measures reassessed posttreatment; 30 of 34 patients who completed the trial provided posttreatment MRI data. At baseline, pBMS patients exhibited elevated ACC Glx/Cr (median 2.51 vs 1.93, P = 0.021) and tNAA/Cr (median 1.97 vs 1.72, P = 0.050) ratios, reduced gray matter volume in the left medial superior frontal gyrus and left frontal pole, and decreased pregenual ACC (pgACC) and subgenual ACC (sgACC)-centered connectivity involving the left middle frontal gyrus and left inferior parietal lobule. Glx/Cr correlated positively with visual analog scale (VAS) scores and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores, and tNAA/Cr correlated negatively with VAS and Central Sensitization Inventory scores. After treatment, the mean VAS reduction was 3.28 points (intention to treat; ITT); 44.74% (ITT, n = 38) and 50.00% (per-protocol, n = 34) attained ≥50% pain relief. The median ACC Glx/Cr decreased from 2.51 to 1.85 (P = 0.008) and pgACC-centered functional connectivity increased, whereas regional gray matter volume-including the pre-existing deficits in the left medial superior frontal gyrus and left frontal pole-showed no significant longitudinal change. In conclusion, pBMS is characterized by metabolic and functional neuroimaging alterations within pgACC and sgACC that covary with symptomatic improvement under low-dose pregabalin, whereas structural deficits remain unchanged in the short term. These exploratory findings support the potential benefits of low-dose pregabalin and highlight pgACC and sgACC as promising regions of interest for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Quality of life impairment in Parkinson's disease with probable REM sleep behavior disorder is primarily linked to fear of falling and anxiety.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is associated with worse quality of life (QoL) in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, it remains unclear whether this relationship is direct or mediated through specific clinical features. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study including 468 patients with PD. QoL was assessed using the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39). Multivariable linear regression and mediation analyses with bootstrapping were performed to identify determinants of QoL and potential indirect associations between probable RBD (pRBD) and QoL. Patients with pRBD had worse QoL and a more severe clinical profile. Fear of falling and anxiety emerged as the strongest independent determinants of QoL, whereas pRBD was not an independent predictor. Mediation analyses demonstrated that the association between pRBD and QoL was largely indirect, with fear of falling and anxiety accounting for much of the observed relationship. Depression, gait impairment, and voice handicap showed moderate mediation effects, whereas global non-motor burden had a limited contribution. The NMSS mood/cognition domain was not a significant mediator. The association between pRBD and QoL appears to involve specific clinical factors rather than global symptom burden.

papers.title: Late cortical dynamics mediate numerosity illusions induced by symmetry.
papers.abstract: Numerosity perception enables us to quickly estimate the number of objects in a visual scene, a fundamental skill supporting efficient interaction with the environment. In this study, we tracked how the human brain transforms physical inputs into numerical percepts. Using EEG, we characterized the temporal dynamics of how numerosity-related signals are integrated with spatial configuration cues that shape perception. We leveraged on a visual illusion in which dot arrays appear less numerous when arranged symmetrically rather than randomly. Participants viewed dot arrays of varying physical or perceived numerosity, illusorily altered by the dots' spatial arrangement. Both univariate and multivariate analyses revealed that physical numerosity was decodable from occipitoparietal electrodes as early as ~50 ms after stimulus onset, independently of low-level features such as convex hull, density, individual and total item area. Spatial arrangement was represented later, from ~150 ms, and perceived numerosity, biased by symmetry-induced grouping, emerged at a similar latency. These results indicate that early neural signals encode physical numerosity directly, whereas the symmetry-induced underestimation arises from late grouping processes, such as those involved in incremental grouping, supporting object segmentation.

papers.title: A synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complex organizes photoreceptor neurotransmission.
papers.abstract: Photoreceptor synapses rely on mitochondria, synaptic ribbons, and vesicles, yet how these elements integrate into functional units remains unclear. Here we show, using focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) and electrophysiology, that they form synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complexes (sMRVcs) with fundamentally different architectures in rods and cones. Rod spherules exhibit a strict 1:1 pairing of a single megamitochondrion with one ribbon, sustaining continuous glutamate release in darkness, whereas cone pedicles contain multiple distributed sMRVcs. Disrupting the mitochondrial anchor protein syntaphilin shifts this ratio to 2:1 in rods, with additional mitochondria recruited near the ribbon, and enhances synaptic transmission. In a retinal degeneration model, the sMRVc progressively disassembles before functional decline, with fragmented mitochondria, detached ribbons, and dispersed vesicles. We also identify non-ribbon release sites selectively targeting horizontal cells. These findings establish the sMRVc as a conserved structural-metabolic module whose subtype-specific organization reflects distinct visual demands and whose integrity is essential for synaptic health.

papers.title: EEG and fNIRS evidence for brain responses to three tannins: implications for astringency surface sub-quality in red wine.
papers.abstract: The astringency surface sub-quality is pivotal to red wine perception, yet its neural bases remain unclear. The approaches of non-invasive neurophysiological techniques, sensory analysis, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis, and molecular docking were applied to examine the astringency surface sub-quality responses to three tannins-tannic acid, grape tannin and wine tannin-standardized to equivalent astringency intensity. The results showed that the three tannins at iso-intensity evoked distinct brain activity and sensory responses (wine tannin > tannic acid > grape tannin). The electroencephalography (EEG) results showed that frontal activation was significantly higher than in other regions, with differential delta-band power, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) revealed corresponding changes in oxygenated hemoglobin across different frontal cortical regions, most prominently at channel 6 in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. LC-MS analysis of tannins indicated that higher levels of tannin oligomers, polymeric pigments and free anthocyanins were associated with finer astringency sub-quality and stronger neurophysiological responses. By establishing a clear link between chemical composition and neural activation, this investigation demonstrates the efficacy of using neurophysiological measures as a robust, objective tool to complement and refine traditional sensory evaluation of wine.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Profiles of Human Pluripotent Stem Cell Lines Harboring Circadian Clock Gene Mutations.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are driven by transcriptional-translational feedback loops (TTFLs) involving core regulators such as CLOCK, BMAL1, and REV-ERBs (NR1D1 and NR1D2), which mediate rhythmic transcription through E-box- and RRE-dependent mechanisms. Although pluripotent embryonic stem cells (ESCs) express core clock components, they do not exhibit functional circadian oscillations, suggesting additional circadian-independent roles for these factors. Here, we present CRISPR/Cas9-engineered human ESC lines carrying targeted truncations in CLOCK, BMAL1, NR1D1, and/or NR1D2, together with their transcriptomic datasets. The mutant lines showed genotype-specific transcriptomic alterations while largely preserving expression of pluripotency-associated genes. These resources provide a platform for investigating non-canonical functions of circadian clock components in human pluripotent cells and for future studies of circadian gene networks in differentiated human cell types and organoid systems.

papers.title: Circadian misalignment reshapes gut microbial rhythms to underlie digestive disorders.
papers.abstract: Daily oscillations generated by the host circadian clock, together with rhythmic processes arising from the gut microbiota, form an integrated temporal framework that shapes digestive physiology. The host circadian clock shapes the gastrointestinal landscape through coordinated regulation of feeding patterns, epithelial renewal, immune surveillance, and bile acid metabolism. In turn, the gut microbiota generates rhythmic metabolites that provide reciprocal feedback to epithelial, metabolic, and immune pathways, further reinforcing circadian organization. Disruption of this bidirectional alignment, whether caused by altered light exposure, irregular eating patterns, genetic variation, or lifestyle-induced circadian misalignment, can fragment microbial oscillations, weaken mucosal resilience, and increase susceptibility to inflammatory, metabolic, and malignant digestive disorders. In this Review, we synthesize emerging insights into the molecular architecture that coordinates host and microbial rhythms and examine how its breakdown contributes to gastrointestinal disease. We also discuss chronobiological interventions, including feeding schedules, pharmacological timing, and microbiota-targeted strategies, that aim to restore temporal alignment. Viewing time as a critical functional dimension of host-microbiota biology provides a conceptual foundation for advancing precision diagnostics and therapeutics in digestive health.

papers.title: Comprehensive review of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome.
papers.abstract: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) is a complex, debilitating disease that is unexplained and is characterised by persistent unexplained fatigue, Post Exertional Malaise (PEM), cognitive impairment, unrefreshing sleep and multisystem impairment. Despite the high burden of symptoms and the worldwide prevalence, ME/CFS has been poorly understood, underdiagnosed and underfunded. This large-scale review summarises the available evidence regarding the epidemiology, diagnostic progress, main clinical characteristics, pathophysiological theories and therapeutic approaches for ME/CFS. Despite problems with diagnostic consistency, the lack of validated biomarkers, and historical linkage to psychiatric illness, the recognition of this condition has been delayed and has led to patient marginalisation. The review highlights PEM as a cardinal symptom and reviews the weaknesses in earlier diagnostic criteria, as well as current changes in treatment guidelines, including the formal withdrawal of Graded Exercise Therapy, which has evidence of harm. New pathophysiological evidence suggests mitochondrial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, autonomic imbalance, neuroinflammation, and alterations in gut microbiome. New diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, such as metabolomic and electrophysiological assays, mTOR inhibitors, and decentralised clinical trial designs, are being studied. This intersection with Long COVID offers a chance to rapidly advance studies of post-infectious chronic diseases. The paper also argues for stringent subtyping, uniform data collection, and ongoing patient participation in research as strategies to surmount challenges of heterogeneity. Finally, it underscores the critical need for fair funding of research, so biomarker discovery and development of disease-modifying treatments can be achieved. The care of people with ME/CFS is not only a clinical obligation, but also a public health one.

papers.title: Association between fibromyalgia and severity of coronary artery disease assessed by SYNTAX score: a cross-sectional study of 347 patients.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a prevalent pain syndrome that causes chronic pain, tenderness, sleep disturbance, and impaired function. It shares risk factors for coronary artery disease (CAD), such as obesity, diabetes, rheumatic diseases, and depression. Moreover, FM and CAD could have an independent association. We aimed to evaluate the association between FM and the severity of CAD. This cross-sectional study was performed on 347 patients who underwent coronary angiography. The participants were divided into three groups based on their SYNTAX score. Group A (n = 130) had normal angiography, Group B (n = 152) had a SYNTAX score ≤ 22, and Group C (n = 65) had a SYNTAX score > 22. All patients were evaluated for FM based on the 2016 ACR criteria. A total of 59 (17.0%) patients were identified as having FM. The results showed Group C had higher prevalence of older individuals, males, diabetes, dyslipidemia, FM, and lower levels of vitamin D and physical activity among the groups. After adjusting the findings for age, sex, diabetes, physical activity, LDL level, and level of vitamin D, the multivariable logistic regression test showed that FM is associated with approximately a 26.4-fold higher odds of severe CAD (SYNTAX score > 22) (p < 0.001, OR: 26.38, CI95%: 7.41-93.90). Our findings indicated that FM was independently associated with substantially higher odds of severe CAD (SYNTAX score > 22) after adjustment for prespecified demographic and clinical covariates. Not applicable.

papers.title: Hair cortisol as a marker of physiologic stress in residency training.
papers.abstract: Hair cortisol analysis allows assessment of long-term cortisol exposure and may provide insight into chronic hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activation in medical residents and residency on-call responsibilities. To determine the hair cortisol concentration (HCC) representing 3 months of medical residency and secondarily, its association with various on-call models (in-hospital, night float, home call and no call). Cross-sectional study of 66 medical residents who were recruited to provide hair samples collected after a three-month block in medical residency. Academic, tertiary health care system. Volunteer sample of first through third year medical and primary care residents. Three cm of hair was divided into 3 segments of 1 cm each; each segment represented 1 month of cumulative cortisol production. HCC results were compared to a published, cortisol assay-specific normative population reference interval. HCC results were interpreted according to a priori categorizations of moderate (+ 1.5SD), considerable (+ 2SD) or extreme ( > + 3SD) HCC elevations. Associations with various on-call models were an exploratory secondary outcome. The median age was 28 (26-30) years with median sleep duration of 2 h on in-hospital call. 40% of trainees had at least one HCC segment above the threshold deemed marked elevation. Median HCC was significantly higher for in-hospital and night float vs. no call (285 ng/g and 335 ng/g vs. 78 ng/g p < 0.05) and approached significance compared to home call (190 ng/g, p = 0.06). We have described chronic exposure to endogenous cortisol in medical residency. Nearly half of trainees experienced at least one month of severe hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation in a 3-month timeframe; many had marked chronic cortisol elevations across the entire 3 month observation frame. HCC was higher in months where in-hospital on-call was required. This may have implications for long-term health of trainees and raises questions about the structure of duty hours and sequence of care acuity blocks within residency training programs.

papers.title: Suicidal behavior and subjective mental well-being among conflict-affected high school students in the North Wollo Zone, Ethiopia: a multilevel analysis.
papers.abstract: Adolescents living in conflict-affected areas have higher rates of suicidal behaviors and lower subjective mental well-being than adolescents living outside war-affected areas. However, the extent of the problem might be much greater than we can imagine in northern Ethiopia due to severe impacts of the war among high school students. This study aimed to examine the predictors of suicidal behavior and subjective mental well-being among high school students in conflict-affected areas in the North Wollo Zone, Ethiopia. A school-based cross-sectional survey was carried out among 3400 high school students in the North Wollo Zone, Ethiopia. Multistage stratified random sampling was used to recruit study participants. The analysis focused on two binary outcome variables: suicidal behavior and subjective mental well-being. Multilevel logistic regression analysis was used to identify factors influencing students' suicidal behaviors and poor mental well-being. In the final model, all significance tests with a p-value < 0.05 were considered significant factors associated with suicidal behaviors and poor mental well-being. The prevalence of suicidal behaviors was 6.9%, and nearly one-third (33.5%) of high school students struggled with poor subjective mental well-being. The final analysis revealed significant associations: female sex, family residence, post-traumatic stress disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder were associated with both suicidal behavior and poor subjective mental well-being. Suicidal behavior was associated with poor sleep and poor subjective mental well-being, whereas low academic performance, large class size and suicidal behavior were associated with poor mental well-being. High school students living in conflict-affected areas reported high levels of suicidal behavior and poor subjective mental well-being. This highlights the urgent need to prioritize mental and psychosocial support, and ensuring access to services is a critical and urgent component.
papers.journal: International journal of mental health systems

papers.title: MiR-182 regulates IL-6 and HCN4 in the cardiac context: implications for human atrial electrical remodelling.
papers.abstract: The progression of cardiac electrical remodelling and the onset of proarrhythmic events are multifactorial processes, with many factors contributing to atrial electrical remodelling and the consequent development of atrial fibrillation (AF). Recently, miR-182 has been identified as causative factors of arrhythmogenesis in animal models but its potential relationship with proinflammatory mediators such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), emerged as new key player in independent preclinical evidence for atrial electrogenesis, remains unknown. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) were differentiated into cardiomyocytes (CMs) to study the role of miR-182-overexpression (OE) in human cardiac background. Functional consequences were assessed by measuring spontaneous electrical activity by using MULTIPLE-High-Throughput and Intracell systems, with/without autonomic stimulation. Molecular analyses by RT-PCR/Elisa assays were performed. Hearts from the Tg(myl7:GAL4,EGFP)xTg(Sce.4xUAS: miR-182,cry: EGFP) zebrafish line [Tg(myl7 > miR-182)] were used to measure the expression of dre-il6. Human IL-6 protein (5,4 pg/nL) was microinjected in the pericardial region of 2dpf Tg(myl7:EGFP) wt-like zebrafish embryos and heart rate was recorded. Expression analyses were performed on human left atrial samples of 49 patients (11 controls, CT; 18 left atrial dilation (LA-D); 20 permanent AF). MiR-182-OE in hiPS-CMs significantly impact cardiac electrophysiology showing reduced and irregular spontaneous beating rate. Accordingly, MiR-182-OE downregulated the expression of HCN4, encoding for the pacemaker f-current, incrementing IL-6 expression and secretion and via ISL1. On the contrary, 24-48 h incubation with IL-6 (50ng/mL) did not change miR-182-5p expression levels in CT hiPS-CMs. The IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab (TOC, 10 µg/mL) partially rescued HCN4 expression in miR-182-OE hiPS-CMs. Interestingly, miR-182-OE in hiPS-CMs enhanced response to acetylcholine and dysregulated genes associated with atrial pathology. Zebrafish heart samples from Tg(myl7 > miR-182) exhibited increased il6 expression levels. Pericardial injection of human IL-6 in wt zebrafish embryos decreased heart rate. Finally, miR-182-5p was found to be overexpressed in human biopsies from patients with LA-D, with the highest expression levels observed in patients with permanent AF; remarkably, miR-182 levels were positively correlated with IL-6 expression. The results support the hypothesis of a causative link between miR-182-OE and IL-6 production in the cardiac context. This molecular axis may represent an associated molecular signature predisposing to arrhythmogenesis. Overall, our findings reveal novel pathophysiological mechanisms concordant across models and suggest novel pharmacological targets within the complex AF setting.

papers.title: Latent profile analysis-based development and validation of a model for differentiating subjective cognitive decline profiles in older hemodialysis patients: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Subjective cognitive decline is often discussed as a potential early marker of dementia. Although subjective cognitive decline has been proposed as a key early warning sign of preclinical Alzheimer's disease, it is important to recognize that subjective cognitive decline as a subjective perception is strongly influenced by psychological state, social environment, and physical health. Older maintenance hemodialysis patients are at high risk for subjective cognitive decline due to uremic toxin accumulation, dialysis-related brain injury, and multiple comorbidities. Traditional total-score-based assessments fail to capture the intrinsic heterogeneity among Subjective cognitive decline subgroups. Latent profile analysis, a person-oriented approach, can identify latent subgroups with similar multidimensional characteristics. Given the insidious nature of subjective cognitive decline and the differential characteristics across profiles, constructing profile-specific classification models is crucial for timely risk screening. To explore the latent profiles of subjective cognitive decline in older maintenance hemodialysis patients, analyze characteristic differences and associated factors among these profiles, and develop and evaluate a classification model for differentiating subjective cognitive decline profiles in this population. Using convenience sampling, 300 older maintenance hemodialysis patients from Li Huili Hospital of Ningbo Medical Center, Zhejiang Province, China, between May and November 2025 were recruited. Participants completed a general information questionnaire, the subjective cognitive decline Questionnaire-9, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and the Short Physical Performance Battery. Latent profile analysis was performed based on the subjective cognitive decline Questionnaire responses. Univariate analysis and multinomial logistic regression were used to construct the classification model. The model's performance was comprehensively evaluated across three dimensions: authenticity, reliability, and discriminatory ability. Two hundred seventy-five valid questionnaires were collected and latent profile analysis identified three distinct subjective cognitive decline profiles: Mild Cognitive Decline Group (C1, 40.00%), Moderate Cognitive Decline Group (C2, 38.18%), and Severe Cognitive Decline-Physical Dysfunction Group (C3, 21.82%). The classification model for subjective cognitive decline in older maintenance hemodialysis patients, constructed using multivariate regression analysis, demonstrated a good fit in the Hosmer-Lemeshow test (P > 0.05). Furthermore, it exhibited outstanding discriminatory performance in terms of validity, reliability, and discriminatory ability. Subjective cognitive decline among older maintenance hemodialysis patients is prevalent at a moderate-to-high level and demonstrates significant heterogeneity, classifiable via latent profile analysis into three distinct profiles. The classification model incorporating dialysis vintage, monthly social activity participation hours, serum albumin, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and the Short Physical Performance Battery scores demonstrates significant discriminatory efficacy within the derivation sample, offering a preliminary foundation for risk stratification in this high-risk population that warrants external validation.

papers.title: Nine-month changes in growth, bone age, and biochemical growth markers following adenotonsillectomy in children with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome: a prospective single-arm study.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated nine-month changes in anthropometric growth, skeletal maturation, and biochemical growth markers following adenotonsillectomy in children with OSAS. This prospective single-center, uncontrolled before-and-after study included 50 children aged 3-12 years with OSAS who underwent adenotonsillectomy. OSAS severity was assessed preoperatively using Type III home respiratory polygraphy. Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ) scores, anthropometric measurements, Greulich-Pyle bone age, and serum IGF-1, IGFBP-3, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin, sclerostin, and Dickkopf-1 (DKK-1) levels were evaluated before surgery and at nine months. The median [IQR] PSQ score decreased from 10.0 [3.3] preoperatively to 3.0 [2.0] postoperatively (p < 0.001), while height percentile and BMI Z-score increased. Preoperative REI correlated positively with PSQ score (r = 0.383; p = 0.003). Using a six-month BA - CA threshold, preoperative skeletal maturation was classified as delayed in 34.0%, normal in 42.0%, and advanced in 24.0% of participants. The mean paired change in BA - CA was 0.28 years (95% CI, 0.17-0.39; p < 0.001). BMI Z-score gains were greater in children who were underweight or healthy weight at baseline. IGF-1 and ALP levels increased, whereas sclerostin and DKK-1 levels decreased (all p < 0.001); IGFBP-3 and osteocalcin remained unchanged. An exploratory ROC analysis of preoperative sclerostin yielded an AUC of 0.760 (95% CI, 0.611-0.909; p = 0.013) for discriminating advanced bone age. Adenotonsillectomy was followed by reduced symptom burden and changes in anthropometric measures and skeletal maturation. Changes in sclerostin and DKK-1 provide preliminary data regarding Wnt-related bone metabolism in pediatric OSAS, although their clinical significance requires validation in larger controlled studies.

papers.title: Tongue Base Collapse as an Independent Risk Factor for CPAP Non-Compliance in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea.
papers.abstract: While nasal airway influencing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) treatment compliance is well-described, the impact of pharyngeal airway collapse patterns on CPAP compliance remains relatively unexplored. The relationship between tongue base collapse and CPAP compliance was evaluated. A single-centre retrospective cohort study was conducted reviewing consecutive adults with obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) who underwent drug-induced sleep endoscopy between 01/10/2024 and 01/10/2025 for consideration of CPAP alternatives. Severe tongue base collapse was defined as Tb2 (> 50% collapse) using the PTLTbE classification. CPAP non-compliance was defined as failure to use CPAP for ≥ 4 h on ≥ 70% of nights in the preceding 30 days. Associations were analysed with logistic regression, with Firth penalised regression as a sensitivity analysis. Seventy-five patients were included; 43 (57.3%) were CPAP non-compliant. Severe tongue base collapse was more frequent in the non-compliant group (p = 0.031), and associated with increased odds of CPAP non-compliance (OR 4.67, 95% CI 1.46-16.20; p = 0.011). This association persisted after adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, apnoea-hypopnoea index and other anatomical collapse sites (adjusted OR 7.17, 95% CI 1.56-40.99; p = 0.016; AUC 0.811), and with Firth regression (adjusted OR 4.72, 95% CI 1.23-21.69; p = 0.023). A significant linear trend was observed across increasing tongue base collapse grades (adjusted OR per Grade 2.68, 95% CI 1.25-6.35; p = 0.016). Total collapse burden was not associated with CPAP compliance. In patients evaluated for CPAP alternatives, severe tongue base collapse was independently associated with CPAP non-compliance. Our findings suggest OSA endotypes may merit consideration in understanding CPAP compliance.
