papers.title: Standards to Support Healthy Sleep for Pediatric Inpatients and Their Families: A Delphi Survey.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for physical and mental health. However, its importance is often overlooked in hospitals, negatively impacting children's well-being and recovery as well as their caregivers' ability to provide support. The aim of this study was to achieve consensus on internationally relevant standards to promote healthy sleep in hospitals providing pediatric in-patient care. An expert steering group developed 32 potential standards for supporting child and caregiver sleep in hospitals based on research, clinical experience, and surveys of pediatric sleep groups. A panel formed from the International Pediatric Sleep Association (IPSA) membership completed a 3-round Delphi study to guide the development of 5 to 15 final standards. Consensus was defined as at least 80% agreement using a 4-point Likert scale. Narrative comments were incorporated. Seventy-six multiprofessional participants from 23 countries/regions consented to participate. A panel of 49 were selected, maximizing geographical and professional representation, to complete rounds 2 and 3, with 35 (71%) from 20 countries/regions and 23 (47%) from 13 countries/regions participating, respectively. Consensus was high throughout. The final round organized the information into 5 overarching standards encompassing sleep included in the health care plan, commitment from senior management, promotion of circadian rhythms, family support, and environmental modifications. Each standard had 5 or 6 associated criteria. The standards achieved 96% agreement. Consensus was achieved on 5 overarching standards with their associated criteria designed to facilitate stepwise change, be adaptable to local contexts, and provide measurable outcomes to support healthy sleep for hospitalized children and families globally.
authors: Sleep-Friendly Hospitals Task Force, on behalf of the International Pediatric Sleep Association (IPSA) Board of Directors

papers.title: Climate change, place, and mental health in sub-Saharan Africa: A multi-country analysis of lived experiences following extreme weather events.
papers.abstract: Climate change is an escalating global health threat, with sub-Saharan Africa disproportionately affected due to entrenched spatial inequalities, high exposure to environmental hazards, and limited adaptive capacity. Increasingly frequent extreme weather events (EWEs), including floods and cyclones, are reshaping the material and social conditions of place, with implications for mental health and wellbeing. However, evidence remains limited, particularly multi-country qualitative research that examines how mental health impacts are produced through lived experiences of place in contexts of recurring environmental disruption and structural vulnerability. This study explored the mental health and wellbeing impacts of EWEs among individuals with lived experience of such events in Mozambique, Burkina Faso, South Africa, and Kenya, using participatory methods that centred community narratives and place-based accounts of everyday life. This qualitative study employed digital storytelling as a participatory visual method to examine how EWEs are experienced and narrated across diverse socio-spatial contexts. A total of 37 participants (8-10 per country) were recruited from rural, peri-urban, and informal urban settlements with recent exposure to flooding or cyclone events. Participants produced digital stories during facilitated five-day workshops. These narratives were analysed using inductive and deductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke's framework, with attention to the spatial and relational production of distress and coping. Across Mozambique, Burkina Faso, South Africa, and Kenya, findings show that the mental health impacts of EWEs are deeply embedded in place-based conditions and are cyclical, cumulative, and relational rather than confined to discrete disaster events. Participants described how repeated environmental disruptions reconfigured everyday life in place, generating ongoing uncertainty, anticipatory anxiety during rainfall periods, and acute fear during floods and cyclones. Loss of housing, livelihoods, infrastructure, and social anchors of place contributed to enduring psychological distress, which was frequently reactivated by subsequent environmental cues such as heavy rain, wind, and deteriorating physical environments. Persistent anxiety, hypervigilance, sleep disturbance, and emotional distress were reported across all sites. While social and community networks constituted critical infrastructures of care within place, these were often simultaneously overwhelmed as entire communities experienced shared disruption. Limited and delayed institutional responses further compounded spatial and social precarity. This study provides a comparative participatory account of how EWEs shape mental health through their embeddedness in place across diverse sub-Saharan African contexts. The findings demonstrate that psychological distress is produced through the interaction of repeated environmental exposure, structural inequality, and disrupted place-based infrastructures of daily life, rather than emerging solely as a post-disaster outcome. These results underscore the need for climate-responsive mental health and psychosocial support that is integrated into place-based disaster risk governance, alongside strengthened social protection and community infrastructure that can sustain wellbeing in contexts of recurring environmental instability.

papers.title: 12-month trajectories of anxiety symptoms and functional recovery after new-onset stroke: A multicenter prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: The longitudinal course of poststroke anxiety remains poorly characterized. This study aimed to delineate the trajectories of anxiety symptoms within 12 months post-stroke and evaluate their associations with functional recovery. This prospective multicenter cohort study enrolled patients with new-onset stroke from 2018 to 2021. Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the 14-item Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA) at 2 weeks and at 3, 6, and 12 months. Latent class growth modeling and growth mixture modeling identified latent trajectory classes. Multivariate logistic regression evaluated the association between anxiety trajectory and 12-month functional outcome (modified Rankin scale). Among 1934 patients (1357 males; mean age 58.8 ± 10.9 years), the median initial HAMA score was 8 (4,13). Two distinct anxiety trajectories were identified: a low-decreasing group (1538 [79.5%]) with mild, descending symptoms (intercept, 8.400; mean difference, -3.510), and a high-increasing group (396 [20.5%]) characterized by escalating and persistent anxiety, with changes occurring predominantly within the first 3 months (intercept, 12.508; mean difference, 4.471). Female, moderate-to-severe stroke, depressive symptoms, poor sleep, and low resilience were independent risk factors of the high-increasing trajectory (all p < 0.01). Crucially, this trajectory was significantly associated with poor functional recovery at 12 months (aOR, 2.24; 99% CI, 1.58-3.17). A trajectory of increasing and persistent anxiety, identified in one-fifth of acute stroke patients, was independently associated with 12-month disability. These findings necessitate a paradigm shift from static, cross-sectional assessment to longitudinal tracking of anxiety symptoms, particularly during the first 3 months post-stroke, to improve functional outcomes.

papers.title: An ecological momentary assessment of the reciprocal association between short-term sleep-wake variability and binge eating.
papers.abstract: Research suggests an association between sleep and eating disorder (ED) behaviors; we sought to identify whether variable sleep-wake patterns and binge eating predict each other. We tested the bidirectional association between sleep and binge eating among university students with binge eating and sleep disruptions (N = 64) using a 1-week ecological momentary assessment (EMA) design. Participants completed daily food and sleep diaries and reported binge-eating episodes. Generalized linear mixed models tested whether between- and within-person sleep-wake variability (bedtime, waketime, and circadian midpoint) predicted next-day binge eating (and vice versa). Most participants met DSM-5 criteria for a lifetime (95.16%) and current (91.94%) ED; 43.55% met criteria for insomnia or hypersomnia. At the within-person level, sleep-wake variability did not predict next-day binge eating (or vice versa). At the between-person level, greater overall waketime and circadian midpoint variability were associated with a decreased odds of binge eating across the EMA period. Thus, individuals whose waketimes and circadian midpoints shifted more from one day to the next had a reduced likelihood of binge eating. Post-hoc analyses indicated that 68.3% of the sample engaged in at least one night of catch-up sleep (≥ 7 hours following a night of short sleep). Findings suggest a link between sleep-wake variability and binge eating that warrants further study. Findings may be driven by short sleepers who benefit from catch-up sleep that leads to greater sleep-wake variability. The influence of sleep and binge eating may be cumulative, warranting longer monitoring than occurred in this brief EMA period.

papers.title: Exploring the impossible: Prior sleep timing and infants' response to violation-of-expectation events.
papers.abstract: Infants actively explore their environment to learn. Events that contradict infants' prior experiences about how the world works are thought to serve as special learning opportunities. Infants preferentially explore objects behaving in an unusual way and test their properties related to the event. Given the critical role of sleep in infant cognition, we hypothesized that the exploratory response to events that violate basic physical principles would vary depending on prior sleep timing. Eight- to 12-month-old infants (n = 28) viewed televised events either shortly after a nap or following prolonged wakefulness. Each infant saw one object violate the law of object solidity and another object conform with it. Immediately afterward, infants showed targeted exploration of the object violating solidity: they explored it longer than the experience-conforming object and a novel distractor, and they were more likely to test its properties regarding the violated principle. Unexpectedly, there was no significant effect of prior sleep timing on how infants explored the objects. However, exploratory regression analyses revealed that longer prior wakefulness duration was associated with less targeted exploration of the object violating solidity. Additional studies are required to test if prior sleep timing is associated with how infants process and respond to physically impossible events in confirmatory analyses.

papers.title: Screen-based sedentary behaviors and depression: differential associations of TV/Video viewing and computer use.
papers.abstract: Screen-based sedentary behaviors may be modifiable contributors to depression. We examined whether TV/video viewing and computer use differ in their associations with depression. We analyzed 20,207 adults from four National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles (2005-2006, 2011-2012, 2013-2014, and 2015-2016). Participants reported average daily TV/video viewing and computer use over 30 days; depression was defined as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score ≥10. Survey-weighted categorical, continuous, standardized, mutually adjusted, restricted cubic spline, model-based time-reallocation, subgroup, survey-cycle, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Compared with none or <1 h/day, ≥5 h/day of TV/video viewing and computer use were associated with higher depression odds [odds ratio (OR), 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.69 (1.33-2.14) and 1.58 (1.19-2.09), respectively]. In mutually adjusted continuous models, estimates per 1 h/day were 1.19 (1.11-1.27) and 1.06 (0.99-1.13), respectively. Associations were nonlinear. At fixed total TV-plus-computer time, model-based reallocation of 1 h/day from TV/video viewing to computer use yielded 0.89 (0.80-0.99); the reverse was 1.12 (1.01-1.25). Interactions by sex, age, or body mass index were nonsignificant. Categorical TV/video associations varied by survey cycle, but continuous interactions were nonsignificant. Alternative referents and continuous PHQ-9 outcomes supported the high-exposure pattern; sleep adjustment had little effect, whereas employment adjustment attenuated associations. TV/video viewing showed a stronger association with depression than computer use, with nonlinear patterns across duration. The reallocation estimates are statistical simulations from cross-sectional data, not effects of a longitudinal intervention. Prospective studies incorporating contemporary screen modalities are needed.

papers.title: Intranasal embelin-nanostructured lipid carrier with β-cyclodextrin inclusion complex (EBCD) produces sustained behavioural control of convulsive activity in the lithium-pilocarpine rat model: A behavioural and neurochemical comparison with intranasal diazepam.
papers.abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency requiring rapid behavioural control of convulsive activity. First-line benzodiazepines are frequently administered through delayed or invasive routes, and lose effectiveness as seizure persist. This study evaluated an intranasal embelin-β-cyclodextrin nanostructured lipid carrier (EBCD) as a behavioural proof-of-concept treatment in the lithium-pilocarpine rat model, using intranasal diazepam as reference. Treatment was withheld until continuous Racine stage 3-5 activity had been confirmed behaviourally. Seizures were scored for 60 min using modified Racine scale, and whole-tissue hippocampal GABA, glutamate, and acetylcholine quantified by LC-QTOF-MS; acetylcholine in the treated groups fell below the lowest calibrator and untreated-control glutamate exceeded the highest; both are semi-quantitative. Of 24 rats, 16 developed SE and were assigned to untreated control (n = 4), intranasal diazepam (n = 6), or intranasal EBCD (n = 6). Both treatment groups achieved sustained control of convulsive activity in all animals, whereas none of the untreated rats did (log-rank P = 0.0076). Seizure burden fell in both treated groups, significantly for diazepam versus untreated SE (adjusted P = 0.006) but not for EBCD (adjusted P = 0.10), the EBCD-diazepam difference was not significant (adjusted P = 0.83). The study was not powered as a non-inferiority comparison and does not establish equivalence. Hippocampal glutamate was elevated in untreated SE and reduced by both treatments (P = 0.014), indicating reduced glutamatergic tone, and GABA did not differ. These findings demonstrate that intranasal EBCD merits evaluation in a video-EEG-confirmed dose-response study supports its further development as a rapid nose-to-brain intranasal therapy.

papers.title: Childhood emotional neglect modulates emotional face processing in healthy young adults: An ERP study.
papers.abstract: Childhood Emotional Abuse (EA) and Emotional Neglect (EN) have been proposed to have long-term effects on emotion processing and their neurophysiological correlates in a wide range of clinical populations, yet evidence from non-clinical samples remains limited. The aim of this study is to examine associations between childhood EA and EN and early perceptual (P100, N170) and later evaluative (late positive potential, LPP) stages of emotional face processing in healthy young adults. Fifty-four participants (15 M) (Mean age: 23.9; SD: 3.83) from the Puglia region (Italy) completed a facial emotion categorization task while their neurophysiological activity was recorded through a 32-channel EEG. Childhood EA and EN were retrospectively assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Event-related potential (ERP) peaks, latencies and amplitudes were analyzed using repeated-measures linear mixed-effects models with EA and EN as continuous predictors. EN, but not EA, was associated with increased P100 amplitude across facial expressions [F(1,54) = 7.46, p = .008, ηp2 = 0.121] and shorter N170 latency [F(1,54) = 4.27, p = .044, ηp2 = 0.073]. For the LPP, a significant EN × Emotional Valence interaction emerged [F(2,108) = 3.68, p = .029, ηp2 = 0.064], with a stronger negative association between EN and LPP amplitude for happy than for angry faces; Behaviourally, an EN × Emotional Valence interaction emerged for reaction time [F(2,5954.2) = 4.12, p = .016, ηp2 = 0.001], with slower responses to neutral faces at higher EN and for accuracy. Also, a Valence interaction with both EN [χ2(2) = 13.99, p < .001] and EA [χ2(2) = 17.71, p < .001] emerged. More in detail, the more the EN is, the higher accuracy for happy faces is, while the more EA is, the higher accuracy for angry faces is. Overall, EN was associated with variation across both early and late stages of emotional face processing, whereas EA showed no detectable ERP associations. At the behavioral level, both EN and EA showed valence-specific associations with accuracy (higher accuracy for happy and angry faces, respectively), and EN was additionally associated with slower responses to neutral faces. These preliminary findings suggest that, even in a non-clinical sample, childhood EN is more closely associated with the temporal dynamics of emotional face processing than EA.

papers.title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Excessive Daytime Sleepiness in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) is a common but often overlooked condition in older adults, and it is associated with a variety of adverse outcomes. This study aimed to explore the pooled prevalence of EDS and its risk factors among older adults. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Adults aged 60 years and older in any setting. A systematic search was conducted in 8 databases, including CNKI, VIP, CBM, WanFang Data, Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, and The Cochrane Library from inception to October 2025. Two researchers independently screened the literature and extracted the information. Pooled prevalence estimates and odds ratios for the prevalence of EDS in older adults and its risk factors were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models. Forty-three eligible studies were included; the overall pooled prevalence of EDS in older adults was 16.9%. Subgroup analyses revealed significant variations in prevalence across geographic regions (P < .001), with the lowest rate observed in East Asia (13.0%) and the highest in Western Asia (21.8%). Furthermore, the use of different Epworth Sleepiness Scale cutoff values resulted in significant differences. Several factors were significantly associated with an increased risk of EDS, including male sex, obesity, malnutrition, urinary incontinence, and various comorbidities (eg, dementia, Parkinson's disease, cerebrovascular disease, depression, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, insomnia, and obstructive sleep apnea). Conversely, the use of hypnotic medications may serve as a protective factor. EDS is common among older adults, although prevalence estimates vary across geographic regions and according to the Epworth Sleepiness Scale cutoff used. Several demographic, nutritional, and health-related factors were associated with EDS. These findings support greater clinical attention to EDS and targeted early screening, particularly among older adults with relevant comorbidities or other associated factors, to facilitate timely evaluation and appropriate intervention.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association

papers.title: Characterizing the heterogeneity of Alzheimer's disease through EEG normative modeling.
papers.abstract: To integrate normative modeling with non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) to characterize individualized brain functional abnormalities across Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), thereby elucidating disease heterogeneity and enabling biologically informed stratification. We constructed sex-specific normative age models for the small-world (SW) architecture of hemispheric EEG networks and quantified individual SW deviations in 160 AD, 161 MCI, and 769 healthy controls (HCs) across multiple datasets. Individual deviation profiles were used to delineate sex-dependent topological alterations across the cognitive spectrum. We further performed unsupervised clustering to identify subtypes for both AD and MCI, and characterized their inter-subtype similarities and differences. The identified subtypes were rigorously validated for internal/external consistency and specificity. EEG normative models (NMs) captured frequency-specific aging trajectories of SW organization and revealed progressive sex-related divergence in SW deviation with cognitive decline. Both MCI and AD cohorts were consistently classified into two EEG-defined subtypes with distinct intrinsic dysconnectivity patterns and cognitive profiles, despite no differences in canonical multimodal MRI measures. Subtype-1 exhibited relatively preserved network organization and distinctive neurocognitive recovery patterns, whereas subtype-2 showed widespread network disruption and poorer clinical outcomes. Cross-stage analyses demonstrated shared EEG signatures between corresponding MCI and AD subtype pairs, supporting their biological continuity. Multidimensional validation confirmed the robustness and generalizability of our subtyping framework. NM-guided EEG profiling reveals clinically meaningful neurobiological heterogeneity cross the AD spectrum and identifies a high-risk MCI subtype before detectable cerebral atrophy. This framework provides an individualized, non-invasive strategy for early AD subtyping and prognostic stratification.
papers.journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology

papers.title: Novel Accelerated Heart Rate Index (AHRI) and cardiovascular morbidity: A retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Conventional sleep-derived OSA metrics incompletely capture cardiovascular (CV) risk. We evaluated the association between the novel Accelerated Heart Rate Index (AHRI) and CV morbidity. This retrospective cohort study included adults aged ≥40 years who underwent WatchPAT sleep studies through Clalit Health Services between 2015 and 2022. AHRI was defined as the number of heart rate acceleration events per hour of sleep. Participants were followed through December 2025 for the first occurrence of the composite of hospitalization for myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure. Multivariable cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). Sensitivity analyses included Fine-Gray competing-risk models treating death as a competing event. Among 26,553 participants, 2217 CV events occurred during a median follow-up of 4.47 years. Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a nonlinear association between AHRI and the risk of CV morbidity, with the lowest risk at midrange AHRI. Compared with the midrange quartiles (Q2-Q3), both the lowest (Q1) and highest (Q4) AHRI quartiles were associated with higher risks of CV morbidity with adjusted HRs of 1.12 (95% CI 1.01-1.25) and 1.13 (1.02-1.26), respectively. Findings remained consistent in Fine-Gray competing-risk analysis. HRs were higher among individuals with moderate-to-severe OSA (pAHI ≥15 events/h, P for interaction = 0.005) and among those with high hypoxic burden (P for interaction = 0.012). Among individual outcomes, only heart failure hospitalization showed significant associations with low and high AHRI levels. AHRI demonstrated a U-shaped association with CV morbidity, with both low and high AHRI independently associated with increased risk.

papers.title: An investigation into the cognitive influences on caloric-induced cortical alpha suppression and vestibular responsiveness.
papers.abstract: This study examined the relative contributions of cognitive tasking on cortical alpha suppression during the caloric test and assessed its relationship to peak slow‑phase velocity (pSPV). Electroencephalography (EEG) and electronystagmography (ENG) were performed across three experimental conditions: active (real) and sham caloric testing with and without tasking. Suppression of the alpha rhythm (8-13 Hz) was defined as a global reduction in amplitude relative to baseline. The degree of nystagmus was derived from the pSPV measured during the caloric response. EEG and ENG recordings were obtained from 20 healthy adults with no otologic or neurologic history (mean age = 25.1 ± 3.1 years). Tasking (mental arithmetic) resulted in the largest global reduction in cortical alpha suppression, reflecting changes in both periodic and aperiodic components, when compared to no-tasking conditions (p < 0.001), and a group-level increase in pSPV (p = 0.033). Individual changes in periodic alpha features and the aperiodic exponent were not associated with changes in pSPV (p > 0.05). Caloric-induced cortical alpha suppression was mainly influenced by cognitive state rather than peripheral vestibular drive alone. While the effect of tasking on pSPV is well known, the absence of an association between task-related EEG changes in periodic/aperiodic activity and pSPV suggests that cortical activity and vestibulo-ocular reflex output may be influenced by independent mechanisms.

papers.title: Lifestyle Factors and Cardiometabolic Diseases in Middle-Aged and Older Adults: A Mixed Graphical and Bayesian Network Analysis With Sex-Specific Comparison.
papers.abstract: To examine the complex relationships between lifestyle factors and cardiometabolic diseases and to explore sex-specific network structures and dependency patterns among middle-aged and older adults. This cross-sectional study used data from Wave 5 (2020) of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. Lifestyle factors included physical activity, sleep duration, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Cardiometabolic diseases were identified based on self-reported physician diagnoses. Mixed graphical models and Bayesian networks were applied to investigate conditional associations, potential dependency structures, and sex differences. The study was reported according to the STROBE checklist. A total of 18,548 participants were included. In the mixed graphical models, alcohol consumption and physical activity showed the highest bridge expected influence in men, whereas physical activity and smoking were the most influential bridge nodes in women. Network Comparison Tests indicated no significant sex difference in global network strength, whereas network structure differed significantly between men and women. Bayesian network analysis identified a common dependency pattern across sexes involving physical activity, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. Sex-specific dependency patterns were also observed: alcohol consumption, stroke, heart disease, and diabetes were linked in a prominent pattern among men, whereas smoking, heart disease, and stroke were linked among women. In sensitivity analyses incorporating sociodemographic covariates, lifestyle-CMD associations remained evident in the overall sample and among women, whereas the corresponding associations were no longer clearly evident in the male network. Lifestyle behaviours and cardiometabolic diseases showed distinct network association patterns between men and women. However, the male-specific Bayesian network findings were sensitive to the inclusion of sociodemographic covariates and should be interpreted cautiously. These findings provide insights into the complex associations between lifestyle behaviours and cardiometabolic diseases. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to confirm effects and sex differences. Comprehensive, person-centred lifestyle assessment is important for the prevention and management of cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs). Network-based approaches may help identify complex associations between lifestyle behaviours and CMDs, providing insights for sex-sensitive behavioural assessment and risk stratification. No patient or public contribution.

papers.title: A dynamic network analysis of anxiety-related distress within a quality-of-life framework among adults undergoing chemotherapy.
papers.abstract: To understand anxiety-related distress within the quality-of-life context, this study examined how anxiety-related distress is positioned in the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ) framework, and assessed its strongest associations with other quality-of-life factors over time. This secondary analysis of randomized controlled trial data included 390 adults aged ≥ 50 years (63.1% female) who were assessed across six time points: before chemotherapy (baseline, T1) and during chemotherapy (T2-T6). Longitudinal network analysis was used to evaluate the position and associations of anxiety-related distress, represented by worry and tension, within the EORTC-QLQ framework. A baseline network using all 30 EORTC-QLQ items first identified the position of anxiety-related distress. A reduced longitudinal network using key nodes was then estimated to examine contemporaneous, between-person, and temporal associations over time. The baseline network revealed that worry played a central bridging role within the quality-of-life framework. In the reduced longitudinal network, the strongest evidence emerged in the contemporaneous and between-person networks. At the same assessment occasion, worry and tension were positively associated with depressed mood, trouble sleeping, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and financial difficulties. At between-person level, higher average worry was associated with higher average tension, depressed mood, and financial difficulties; while higher average tension was associated with higher average irritability, worry, and difficulty concentrating. In the temporal network, financial difficulties significantly predicted higher subsequent worry but lower subsequent tension. Anxiety-related distress was centrally embedded within the EORTC QLQ framework, with worry serving as a key connector linking emotional, cognitive, sleep-related, and financial concerns. Potential leverage points for supportive care during chemotherapy were identified. ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT05838638; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05838638?term=NCT05838638&rank=1 .
papers.journal: Quality of life research : an international journal of quality of life aspects of treatment, care and rehabilitation

papers.title: High-Density EEG Signatures of Cataplexy in Narcolepsy Type 1.
papers.abstract: Cataplexy, the pathognomonic symptom of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), consists of sudden, emotion-triggered episodes of muscle atonia during wakefulness, with preserved consciousness. Although cataplexy shares features with REM sleep, its neurophysiological nature remains incompletely understood, particularly in humans. We investigated the electrophysiological signature of cataplexy using 128-channels EEG polysomnography in 10 drug-free NT1 adults. We analyzed 73 cataplexy epochs of ~30 seconds from 59 recorded episodes, compared with epochs of quiet wakefulness, N1 sleep, tonic and phasic REM, and direct-entry-REM-sleep. We compared hypnodensity profiles, computed with U-Sleep, of cataplexy and reference states. Regional and topographic spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands, absolute and relative to total power, were compared across states. EEG fingerprint robustness was assessed via within- and between-participant correlation distances. Cataplexy exhibited a distinct EEG profile with intermediate sleep-wake spectral features. Relative power showed scalp-wide reduced beta and increased delta-theta versus wakefulness, alongside elevated posterior beta and scalp-wide reduced theta-delta versus sleep. Absolute power showed increased global field power across most bands, supporting REM-like activity superimposed onto wake desynchronization. Hypnodensity analysis revealed a mixed-state signature combining wake-, REM-, and N1-like probabilities, supporting a hybrid state. Cataplexy differed from direct-entry-REM-sleep, arguing against a simple wake-to-REM transition. Variability analyses indicated greater between-participants than within-participant differences, suggesting partially conserved but individually expressed EEG signatures. Our findings support that cataplexy is a dissociated hybrid brain state reflecting co-activation of REM-like and wake-like synchronizations, constituting a unique pathological state with intermediate electrophysiological features.

papers.title: Association of the 2HELPS2B Score With Impaired Recovery of Consciousness and In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: Persistent impairment of consciousness after sedation withdrawal represents a diagnostic and prognostic challenge in critically ill patients, particularly in the absence of major structural brain injury. The 2HELPS2B score is an established electroencephalographic tool for seizure-risk stratification; however, its association with neurological improvement and mortality remains insufficiently investigated. We conducted an exploratory multicenter retrospective observational study, including 33 critically ill adults with persistent impairment of consciousness, defined as a Full Outline of UnResponsiveness (FOUR) score <7 persisting for more than 72 hours after sedation withdrawal. Patients with major structural brain injury, severe metabolic abnormalities, or incomplete clinical or electroencephalographic records were excluded. All patients underwent clinically indicated 40-minute video-electroencephalography between the fourth and fifth day after sedation withdrawal. Patients were categorized according to their 2HELPS2B score (≥2 versus <2). The primary outcome was failure to demonstrate any increase in FOUR score during ICU follow-up, and the secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Crude risk ratios (RRs) were calculated, and comparisons were performed using two-sided Fisher's exact tests. Nine (27.3%) patients had a 2HELPS2B score ≥2. Failure to improve FOUR score occurred in four of nine (44.4%) patients with scores ≥2 compared with one of 24 (4.2%) patients with scores <2 (crude RR: 10.67; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.37-83.11; Fisher's exact p=0.013). In-hospital mortality occurred in five of nine (55.6%) patients versus five of 24 (20.8%) patients, respectively (crude RR: 2.67; 95% CI: 1.01-7.07; Fisher's exact p=0.090). CIs were calculated using the approximate logarithmic method. Both estimates were unadjusted and based on a limited number of events. In this small, selected retrospective cohort, a 2HELPS2B score ≥2 was associated with failure to demonstrate improvement in FOUR score during ICU follow-up. Although mortality was numerically higher in the high-score group, the difference was not statistically significant using Fisher's exact test. These preliminary findings do not establish independent prognostic utility or incremental value beyond clinical assessment. Larger prospective studies are required to validate these exploratory associations.

papers.title: AI-Driven Augmented Reality for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: An Emerging Frontier in Diagnosis, Treatment, and Self-Management.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) remains one of the most prevalent yet underdiagnosed chronic disorders worldwide, with persistent challenges in timely diagnosis and long-term adherence to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. Artificial intelligence (AI) and augmented reality (AR) have emerged as promising digital health technologies that address complementary aspects of OSA management. AI has demonstrated strong diagnostic performance under controlled conditions in automated OSA detection, severity classification, and physiological signal analysis, whereas AR is being tested as a way to improve CPAP mask fitting, patient education, and treatment engagement. However, the integration of these technologies has received little attention in either the scientific literature or clinical practice. This commentary highlights the emerging convergence of AI and AR as a novel paradigm for OSA diagnosis, treatment initiation, and self-management. Current evidence indicates that AI-driven AR applications are beginning to appear at the commercial level, yet robust OSA-specific clinical evidence remains limited. Potential applications include AR-guided home diagnostic setup, AI-assisted CPAP mask fitting and desensitization, and personalized AR-based coaching to support long-term treatment adherence. We also discuss key barriers to implementation, including the limited evidence base, algorithmic bias from training data that underrepresent some populations, the privacy of sleep and facial data, the digital divide that affects older and low-income patients, regulatory pathways, and uncertainties regarding clinical integration. Finally, we propose a research agenda, guided by implementation science frameworks, focused on feasibility, usability, patient acceptability, and comparative effectiveness against existing educational and telemedicine approaches, to determine whether AI-driven AR represents a meaningful advance in OSA care. Establishing this evidence base will be essential for translating this emerging technological convergence into routine clinical practice.

papers.title: Seizure Freedom After Focal Epilepsy Surgery in a Child With Tuberous Sclerosis Complex and Coexisting Suspected Subependymal Giant Cell Astrocytoma: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: We report a three-year-old girl with tuberous sclerosis complex and drug-resistant focal epilepsy who achieved clinical seizure freedom after left frontal resection. Seizures began at three months of age and continued despite multiple antiseizure medications, occurring approximately 11-16 times daily. Medical records reported a TSC1 mutation, although the original genetic report was unavailable. Preoperative examination documented developmental delay, absence of spoken language and independent walking, and right-sided hemiparesis graded 4/5. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multiple cortical and subcortical lesions, a prominent left frontal abnormality, and a separate right lateral ventricular lesion considered radiologically suggestive of a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma. Presurgical video-electroencephalography recorded multiple focal motor seizures and subclinical seizure patterns associated with left frontal activity at F3-C3, together with interictal discharges in the same region. Following multidisciplinary assessment, microsurgical resection was performed using neuronavigation, intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, and bipolar stimulation before resection. Intraoperative electrocorticography was not performed. The subsequent neurosurgical record reported the histological diagnosis of the resected frontal specimen as giant cell astrocytoma, grade I; the original pathology report and slides were unavailable for independent review. The separate ventricular lesion remained unresected. At 18-month follow-up, no clinical seizures had been reported since surgery while antiseizure treatment continued. Independent walking and syllabic speech had emerged, although developmental impairment remained. Right-sided hemiparesis was graded 4/5 both before surgery and at follow-up; the intervening postoperative motor course was incompletely documented. Follow-up electroencephalography demonstrated epileptiform activity despite clinical seizure freedom. This case illustrates a favorable seizure outcome after localized surgery in a child with multiple intracranial lesions, while emphasizing the distinction between clinical seizure control, electroencephalographic findings, and reported pathological diagnoses.

papers.title: Exploring the Characteristics of Individuals Taking Sleep Medications Grouped According to the Multimodal Optimized Treatment for Insomnia Framework (MOTIF).
papers.abstract: This study aimed to explore the applicability of the Multimodal Optimized Treatment for Insomnia Framework (MOTIF) among individuals taking sleep medications. We conducted an online survey among individuals from the general population who reported insomnia symptoms and were taking sleep medications. Of the 500 participants, we excluded 126 whose bedtime fell outside the 9:00 PM to 1:00 AM range, and 374 participants were categorized based on time in bed (TIB) and attitudes toward taking sleep medication into four MOTIF groups (A, TIB >6 h, favorable; B, TIB >6 h, unfavorable; C, TIB ≤6 h, favorable; D, TIB ≤6 h, unfavorable). Sleep indices, the Insomnia Severity Index, Patient Health Questionnaire-2, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-2 were compared across groups. Of the 374 participants, 14.4% were clustered into a TIB ≤6 h group. All four MOTIF groups took sleep medications at similar times (approximately 10:30 PM), and insomnia severity and satisfaction with sleep medications did not differ across groups. However, the duration from pills to bedtime was significantly longer in the TIB ≤6 h groups (1.3-1.6 h vs 0.3-0.5 h, p < 0.001). Depression (p = 0.006) and anxiety (p = 0.009) scores were highest in Group C. The actual TIB was 3.1 h shorter than the desired TIB in Group C, compared with 0.0-0.1 h in Groups A and B. Approximately 14% of individuals taking sleep medications had a TIB ≤6 h and were characterized by a longer duration from pills to bedtime. Group C (TIB ≤6 h, favorable) showed the highest depression and anxiety scores.

papers.title: Endothelial Activation and Stress Index is Associated with a Non-Dipping Blood Pressure Pattern in Type 2 Diabetic Patients and Newly Diagnosed Hypertension: A Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: Loss of the normal nocturnal blood pressure fall is an adverse circadian phenotype associated with heightened cardiovascular morbidity. This pattern is particularly prevalent in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), where endothelial impairment, microvascular injury, and autonomic dysregulation frequently coexist. The Endothelial Activation and Stress Index (EASIX), calculated from lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), creatinine, and platelet count, is an accessible laboratory composite integrating cellular injury, renal function, and platelet-related vascular information. This retrospective observational analysis screened consecutive patients with T2DM who underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) between December 2024 and April 2026. After applying predefined eligibility criteria, 380 participants were included: 127 patients with non-dipper hypertension, 127 with dipper hypertension, and 126 normotensive diabetic controls. EASIX was calculated as (LDH × creatinine) / platelet count and transformed using the base-2 logarithm. Statistical analyses included Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc pairwise comparisons, multivariable logistic regression, sensitivity modeling excluding nocturnal blood pressure, incremental discrimination assessment (ΔAUC, net reclassification improvement [NRI], integrated discrimination improvement [IDI]), ROC analysis, bootstrap internal validation, and decision curve analysis. EASIX and log2(EASIX) were significantly elevated in non-dipper hypertensive patients compared with both dipper hypertensive patients (post-hoc adjusted p < 0.001) and normotensive diabetic controls (post-hoc adjusted p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, log2(EASIX) independently predicted non-dipper status after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, HbA1c, absolute nighttime systolic blood pressure, smoking, and coronary artery disease (adjusted OR: 5.864, 95% CI: 3.182-10.809, p < 0.001). In a sensitivity model excluding nighttime systolic blood pressure to prevent potential structural dependence, log2(EASIX) remained an independent predictor (adjusted OR: 5.412, 95% CI: 2.998-9.768, p < 0.001). Adding log2(EASIX) to a baseline clinical model significantly improved discriminative performance (AUC increased from 0.612 to 0.751, ΔAUC = +0.139, p < 0.001), with a continuous NRI of 0.584 (p < 0.001) and an IDI of 0.142 (p < 0.001). In patients with T2DM and newly diagnosed hypertension, elevated EASIX is independently associated with the non-dipper blood pressure pattern and provides incremental predictive value beyond conventional clinical factors. EASIX represents an inexpensive, readily obtainable laboratory composite that may assist in the early risk stratification of diabetic patients requiring detailed ambulatory blood pressure assessment.

papers.title: EEG biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases: Machine learning applications and clinical trial insights.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are diverse conditions characterised by selective dysfunction and progressive loss of neurons, glial cells, and neural networks in the brain and spinal cord. NDs pose a major global health challenge due to ageing populations and lack of cure, prompting interest in developing algorithms for early detection and biomarkers. Electroencephalography (EEG), a non-invasive and cost-effective tool, has emerged as a promising method for identifying neural signatures of NDs. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have further enabled automated diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognostic modelling using EEG data. This review synthesises evidence from 226 studies, mapping the current landscape of EEG-based diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification across various NDs. Unlike prior reviews, it provides a comprehensive overview across multiple disorders, including rare ones, and evaluates the role of ML and AI in clinical translation. We analyse research trends, EEG acquisition and preprocessing, and the development of biomarkers for disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and patient stratification. Spectral power, event-related potentials, and connectivity are the main features, with support vector machines and neural networks as the primary classifiers. We review clinical trials involving EEG in NDs and highlight open-source EEG repositories to support reproducibility and data sharing. Despite promising results, challenges such as small sample sizes, methodological differences, limited model interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation remain. The review highlights the potential of EEG combined with ML/AI for early diagnosis and therapy, while outlining future directions through standardised pipelines, explainable models, and collaborative open data initiatives.

papers.title: Long-term outcomes and quality of life of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and their caregivers.
papers.abstract: Survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at risk of long-term neurological, cognitive, and psychological impairment, and this burden may extend to their caregivers. We evaluated long-term survival and multidimensional outcomes in survivors of refractory OHCA treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and in their caregivers. Adults discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA at a tertiary centre (2013-2024) were included. Survivors underwent long-term assessment of functional status and cognition, and self-reported psychological well-being, sleep, fatigue, return to work, and quality of life (QoL). One caregiver per survivor was evaluated for psychological distress, QoL, fatigue, and perceived burden. Among 406 ECPR-treated patients, 63 (16%) were discharged alive. At a median follow-up of 3.1 (IQR 0.6-6.9) years, 38/62 (61%) were alive, of whom 31 (82%) had favourable neurological outcome. Only 7 of all 406 treated patients (1.7%) were alive with poor neurological outcome. Five-year mortality was higher in patients discharged with poor versus favourable neurological status (86% vs. 13%, p < 0.001). Among the 17 survivors and 19 caregivers assessed, QoL was preserved and comparable between groups (EQ VAS 70 [60-80] vs 80 [75-90]). Most survivors and caregivers reported no limitations in mobility, self-care, or usual activities. Mild cognitive impairment was found in 6/16 survivors and poor sleep quality in 10/17. Anxiety symptoms were more frequent among caregivers than survivors (6/18 vs 1/17). No participant met criteria for symptomatic post-traumatic stress disorder. Seven of 15 previously employed survivors and all caregivers returned to work. Long-term survival after ECPR was largely confined to patients with favourable neurological recovery. Despite preserved overall QoL, survivors frequently showed cognitive impairment and reported sleep disturbances. Anxiety symptoms were common among caregivers. These findings support structured long-term follow-up programmes for both survivors and their families.

papers.title: Obesity and risk of developing obesity related complications and multimorbidity in the US.
papers.abstract: Obesity affects approximately 40% of US adults and is associated with increased risk of obesity-related complications (ORCs). However, comprehensive characterization of obesity-related multimorbidity in the US remains limited. This study evaluates the prevalence, incidence, and progression of ORCs to multimorbidity, as well as associated healthcare costs, across body mass index (BMI) classes. This retrospective observational study used the NorstellaLinQ Real-world Database (January 2017-March 2025). A total of 47 ORCs were assessed across five BMI categories: healthy weight (PwHW), overweight (PwOW), and obesity Classes I-III (OC1-OC3). Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the incidence of ORCs and multimorbidity. Healthcare costs were assessed by BMI category and ORC burden. The study included 3,343,877 individuals, comprising 1,689,728 PwHW and 1,654,149 individuals with overweight or obesity (PwOW, n = 679,834; OC1, n = 490,595; OC2, n = 259,500; and OC3, n = 224,220). The most prevalent baseline ORCs were hypertension (22.90%-61.51%), dyslipidemia (24.52%-50.26%, peak at OC1), and lumbago/lower back pain (20.03%-30.49%). The highest relative hazards of incident ORCs in OC3 were sleep apnea (5.94-fold), polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (4.73-fold), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (4.66-fold), and type 2 diabetes (4.32-fold). People with obesity (PwO) had shorter time to first ORC than PwHW (1.64 months in OC3 vs. 13.93 months in PwHW). Hazards of incident multimorbidity also increased with BMI class, from 1.72-fold (PwOW) to 2.39-fold (OC3) for two incident ORCs and from 1.75-fold to 2.63-fold for three. PwO also incurred higher healthcare costs than PwHW at every ORC burden level, rising further as burden increased. Obesity is associated with higher ORC burden, earlier onset of complications, greater risk of progression to multimorbidity, and higher healthcare costs. These findings support the importance of early identification and optimal management to mitigate the long-term clinical and economic sequelae of obesity.

papers.title: BDNF-mediated amelioration of sleep disruption-induced behavioral disorders by Ginkgo biloba.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruptions linked to adverse outcomes ranging from cognitive decline (e.g., in memory, learning, and sensory integration) to emotional dysregulation (e.g., stress and pathological anxiety). Although pre-sleep cognitive engagement may alleviate some of these effects, effective pharmacological interventions are needed. Ginkgo biloba, a dietary supplement, exerts broad pharmacological actions that support neural function. Here, we investigate hypothesis that Ginkgo biloba counteracts sleep deprivation's detrimental effects by promoting BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity, thereby restoring cognitive and emotional homeostasis. Twenty-eight male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups: sleep disruption (SD) followed by Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg i.p.), sleep-disrupted group only, extract only, and control. The Ginkgo biloba collected from botanical garden of Tehran and the extract was prepared via percolation of plant material with ethanol, followed by evaporation and reconstitution. Animals were subjected to multiple-platform-induced sleep disruption (MPSD) for 2 h/day for 3 consecutive days. Behavioral assessments included the open-field test for stress/anxiety and the Barnes maze for spatial learning and memory over three days. Hippocampal BDNF levels were quantified using ELISA. Intraperitoneal Ginkgo biloba extract improved learning in sleep-disrupted rats, reducing probe-day latency from 71 ± 11 s (deprived) to 38 ± 8 s (p < 0.001); Ginkgo biloba alone yielded 15 ± 8 s. The open-field test revealed a significant increase in both locomotor speed and total distance traveled in the sleep-disrupted rats compared with the other experimental groups (P < 0.001). Sleep disruption reduced hippocampal BDNF from 544.55 ± 23-381.19 ± 17 pm/ml (p < 0.0001). Ginkgo biloba treatment significantly prevented this reduction (557 ± 27 pm/ml; p < 0.001) and, when administered alone, increased BDNF by 20% compared to controls (653 ± 25 pm/ml). Sleep disruption impaired memory and learning but did not significantly affect anxiety. Treatment with Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg) improved memory and reduced anxiety. Hippocampal BDNF changes suggest restorative effects may be mediated by increasing BDNF levels reduced by deprivation. As an Iranian Ginkgo biloba extract was used, further research is needed to identify optimal extraction methods and phytochemical compositions for enhancing BDNF levels, thereby optimizing therapeutic potential of Ginkgo biloba -derived compounds for sleep and cognitive applications.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Multicomponent Non-Pharmacological Interventions for Fibromyalgia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia is a chronic disorder characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbances, and functional and quality-of-life impairment. Its management is complex, and clinical guidelines recommend prioritizing multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions. This systematic review with meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions for fibromyalgia. A literature search of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) published up to August 2026 was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CENTRAL. Outcomes assessed included pain, functional capacity, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and adverse events. Certainty of the evidence (CoE) was assessed using GRADE, and risk of bias using the RoB 2.0 tool. Results were synthesized using meta-analysis or narrative synthesis when heterogeneity required it. Sixty-two RCTs (6983 patients) were included. Compared with control groups (usual care/waiting-list), multicomponent interventions probably produce a small reduction in pain (SMD = -0.25; 95% CI: -0.46 to -0.03; N = 2943) and a moderate improvement in functional capacity (SMD = -0.52; 95% CI: -0.72 to -0.32; N = 2729; CoE: moderate). They may produce a small improvement in HRQoL (physical component: SMD = 0.26; 95% CI: 0.09 to 0.43; N = 543; CoE: high; mental component: SMD = 0.24; 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.43; N = 437; CoE: moderate), and a possible increase in adverse events was observed (RR = 1.95; 95% CI: 1.10 to 3.46; N = 620; CoE: low). When compared with active interventions, multicomponent approaches generally showed little or no effect. Overall, multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions represent a useful therapeutic option for fibromyalgia, especially compared with usual care; however, the CoE is variable, evidence regarding safety remains limited, and higher-quality studies are needed.

papers.title: Short-term multidimensional effects of continuous positive airway pressure in patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome: a single-center retrospective study.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the short-term effects of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) combined with conventional lifestyle intervention on sleep parameters, inflammatory status, hemorheology, vascular endothelial function, upper airway dimensions, and quality of life in patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS). Medical records of 89 patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) treated between July 2023 and September 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. According to management methods, patients were divided into a control group (n=47; receiving lifestyle intervention alone) or a study group (n=42; receiving CPAP plus lifestyle intervention). After 12-week intervention, overall clinical response rates, apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), lowest oxygen saturation (LSaO2), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), upper airway cross-sectional areas, hemorheological parameters, inflammatory cytokines, endothelial function markers, and World Health Organization Quality of Life-BREF questionnaire (WHOQOL-BREF) scores were compared between groups. The overall response rate was higher in the study group than in the control group (92.86% vs. 42.55%, P < 0.001). After treatment, both groups showed improvements in AHI, LSaO2, PSQI, hemorheological parameters, inflammatory cytokines, endothelial function, and quality-of-life scores, with generally greater improvements in the study group (all P < 0.05). Upper airway cross-sectional areas increased in both groups, but between-group differences were not significant. CPAP combined with lifestyle intervention was associated with greater short-term improvements in sleep-related parameters, inflammation, hemorheology, endothelial function, and quality of life in patients with OSAHS. Larger prospective multicenter studies are needed to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Postoperative acute kidney injury following cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass: integration of circadian rhythm and anesthetic factors to develop and validate a predictive model at 7 days.
papers.abstract: To predict postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) following cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) surgery, we developed and validated a nomogram incorporating circadian rhythms and anesthesia-related variables to assist in predicting AKI occurrence. This retrospective analysis included clinical data from 298 patients who underwent cardiac surgery with extracorporeal circulation. All patients were randomly divided into two groups: one for model development (n = 209) and the other for internal validation (n = 89). Candidate variables were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Independent predictors were identified through multivariable logistic regression, and a predictive nomogram was constructed. The model's discriminatory ability, calibration performance, and clinical utility were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Among the 298 patients, 82 developed postoperative AKI, yielding an overall incidence rate of 27.52%. On multivariate logistic regression analysis, undergoing surgery in the afternoon was a protective factor (odds ratio [OR]: 0.482, P < 0.05), whereas preoperative circadian rhythm disturbance, prolonged CPB duration, and increased propofol infusion rate emerged as independent risk factors for postoperative AKI (OR: 3.081, 1.026, and 2.050, respectively; all P < 0.05). The nomogram showed satisfactory discrimination, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.796 (95% CI: 0.728-0.864) in the training set and 0.776 (95% CI: 0.671-0.881) in the validation set. After bootstrap correction with 1,000 resamples, the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.793. At the optimal cutoff point, the sensitivity and specificity for the training cohort were 0.672 and 0.815, respectively, and for the validation cohort, 0.500 and 0.831. Both the training and validation sets showed adequate calibration on the Hosmer-Lemeshow test (P = 0.754 and P = 0.364, respectively). DCA further demonstrated that the nomogram provided a net positive clinical benefit over a wide range of clinically plausible threshold probabilities. The proposed nomogram combines chronobiological factors, anesthesia-related variables, and perfusion time during cardiac surgery. This tool shows potential as a practical means for assessing the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery, though external validation in independent multicenter cohorts is warranted before widespread clinical implementation. In clinical practice, with appropriate validation, this model may help with early risk stratification and aid in designing targeted perioperative intervention measures to reduce the risk of kidney injury in high-risk patients.

papers.title: Lifestyle factors and youth mental health: a network analysis of two national surveys in Korea.
papers.abstract: This study used psychiatric network analysis to examine lifestyle-mental health relationships and identify bridge nodes among Korean young adults. Data from the 2022 (N = 14,966) and 2024 (N = 15,098) Korean National Youth Life Surveys were analyzed using a 14-node Gaussian Graphical Model. Centrality and bridge centrality were estimated, and networks were compared using the network comparison test. Sequential mediation analysis (2000 bootstrap replications) examined the indirect association between smartphone overdependence and suicidal ideation through sleep disturbance, burnout, and depressed mood. Networks were dense in both years, with depressed mood and fatigue showing the highest centrality. Sleep disturbance had the highest bridge centrality in the original networks, but this finding was not robust to exclusion of two binary nodes; poor subjective health emerged as the leading bridge node. No statistically significant differences in global strength or network density were detected between years. Mediation analysis identified a significant indirect association in both years. Lifestyle and mental health factors were interconnected in Korean young adults. Sleep disturbance's bridge ranking was sensitive to node inclusion. Network and mediation findings should be interpreted cautiously and regarded as hypothesis-generating.

papers.title: Efficacy of Zicao Ointment combined with Xiaoyan Topical Granules for the treatment of skin pruritus in hemodialysis patients based on traditional Chinese medicine theory.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical efficacy of Zicao Ointment combined with Xiaoyan Topical Granules in treating skin pruritus among hemodialysis (HD) patients based on traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) external therapy theory. We included 175 HD patients treated at Dongguan Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital from May 2022 to May 2025: 85 received basic treatment (control group) and 90 received Zicao Ointment plus Xiaoyan Topical Granules (research group). The outcome measures included curative efficacy, Visual Analog Scale for Itch (VASI)-based pruritus assessment, Modified Duo's Pruritus Score, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), dialysis adequacy and residual renal function‌ (blood urea nitrogen [BUN], serum creatinine [Scr], β2-microglobulin [β2-MG]), calcium-phosphorus metabolism (serum calcium/phosphorus and parathyroid hormone), serum indices (interleukin [IL]-2/6 and C-reactive protein [CRP]), and safety (contact dermatitis, liver injury, skin irritation/burning sensation, calcium-phosphorus metabolism fluctuation abnormalities). Compared to control patients, those receiving Zicao Ointment plus Xiaoyan Topical Granules had significantly higher overall efficacy, lower VASI, Modified Duo's scores, and PSQI scores at 2 and 4 weeks after treatment, and greater reductions in BUN, Scr, β2-MG, serum phosphorus, iPTH, IL-2, IL-6, and CRP at week 4 (P<0.05). Similar serum calcium and total incidence of adverse events were found in the two groups. Zicao Ointment combined with Xiaoyan Topical Granules based on TCM external therapy theory demonstrates clinical efficacy for treating skin pruritus in HD patients.

papers.title: A Survey of Emergency Department Patients About Outpatient Health and Wellness Coaching.
papers.abstract: Emergency department (ED) patients often have chronic conditions and could benefit from health and wellness coaching. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of adult ED patients from May-July 2026 to assess interest in post-ED health and wellness coaching from 0 (not interested) to 10 (extremely interested). Participants were told coaching would likely cost $100 each for 12 virtual or in-person sessions. We also assessed which areas of health the participants were interested in, barriers to care, perceived effects on return ED use. We had 137/143 respondents that completed the survey and reported their interest in coaching. Median interest in coaching was 0 (IQR, 0-4) with 70 of 137 (51.1%) selecting 0 (not interested). Higher education (beta = 0.49, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.85, P = .009) and PROMIS-10 Global Mental Health T-score (beta = -0.057, 95% CI -0.108 to -0.005, P = .032) were associated with interest in health and wellness coaching. Only 6.5% felt coaching would reduce a subsequent ED visit. Surveyed respondents were most interested in getting help with weight loss, sleep, healthy eating, exercise, and stress management. Post-ED coaching among surveyed ED patients was low despite interest in lifestyle domains used in coaching.

papers.title: Inflammation-Associated Difficult-to-Treat Depression: Biomarkers and Precision Treatment Strategies.
papers.abstract: Difficult-to-treat depression (DTD) remains burdensome despite usual treatment efforts. Inflammation is a potential contributor in a subgroup, but heterogeneous signals, uncertain biomarker thresholds and nonstandardized patient selection limit translation. This invited critical narrative review evaluates mechanisms, biomarkers and treatment evidence to clarify how inflammatory assessment could inform precision psychiatry without overstating causality or clinical readiness. Peripheral inflammatory measures, clinical features and metabolic comorbidity provide complementary but nonspecific information. Their association with persistent symptoms does not establish central neuroinflammation or identify a treatment-responsive endotype. Mechanistic findings implicate interacting neuroimmune, kynurenine, reward and stress pathways, with differing levels of human and preclinical support. Antidepressant-response associations must be distinguished from predictive treatment interactions. Immune-targeted trials provide mixed and preliminary evidence; subgroup or exploratory signals do not override null primary outcomes. The review proposes tiered biomarker assessment and separates established depression and comorbidity care from investigational inflammatory treatment selection. Inflammation-associated DTD is best treated as a provisional stratification concept. Integrating repeated immune measures with clinical and metabolic information may improve the design of prospective treatment trials. Translation requires reproducible assays, validated selection rules, target engagement, patient-important outcomes and adequate safety evaluation. Biomarker-guided strategies must demonstrate benefit beyond usual care before routine implementation across diverse populations.

papers.title: Disentangling Confounders from Pathology in Long-COVID Trajectory Prediction for Women: An Interpretable Large-Language-Model Approach.
papers.abstract: Post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC, "Long COVID") disproportionately affects women, in whom hallmark symptoms-insomnia, fatigue, palpitations, cognitive difficulty-overlap with comorbidities and hormonal transitions such as menopause. This diagnostic overlap is a confounding problem: models that forecast future symptom severity risk attributing baseline physiological noise to viral pathology. We ask whether an interpretable, causally disentangled language model can separate true pathological signal from such confounders while remaining competitive with strong predictors of future PASC severity. Retrospective cohort of 1,155 adult women (median age 61) from the NIH RECOVER program, combining static clinical profiles, longitudinal symptom surveys, and four weeks of mean-aggregated consumer-wearable physiology (heart rate, sleep, activity). We render each patient as a natural-language clinical narrative and fine-tune a small open-weight language model (Qwen2.5-0.5B, LoRA) with an attention-based disentanglement layer that gates the latent state into a causal and a confounder component, trained with an environment-mixing InfoNCE objective. We predict the PASC index at 3-, 6-, and 9-month horizons and benchmark against last-value carry-forward, Lasso, Ridge, gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost), a deep MLP, a tabular ResNet, and a self-attention network, over 20 stratified resamples with paired significance tests. We further stratify by trajectory phenotype (Protected / Responder / Refractory). Long-COVID severity is strongly autocorrelated, so last-value carry-forward is a hard reference and is the most accurate method on the full cohort (MAE 3.02 / 1.99 / 1.52 at 3/6/9 months). Among learned models the LLM regressor had the lowest MAE at every horizon (e.g. 3.11 vs. XGBoost 3.57 at 3 months; paired p ≤ 0.01). In the Responder phenotype- patients whose trajectories actually move-the LLM was the most accurate method overall at 3 and 6 months (MAE 4.72, 4.06), though its advantage over carry-forward was not statistically significant ( p = 0.70, 0.29). The disentanglement layer assigned maximal saliency to direct pathology tokens ( breathlessness, malaise ; 1.00) while suppressing confounders ( menopause, diabetes ; < 0.27) and linguistic filler (< 0.17). For static, slowly evolving patients a simple carry-forward forecast is hard to beat and should be the reference any PASC model is judged against. The value of a learned, disentangled model is (i) better accuracy where trajectories are dynamic and (ii) an interpretable, "clinically honest" attribution that down-weights confounders such as menopause-reducing the risk of misattributing baseline physiology to Long COVID. Long COVID is more common and often more severe in women, but many of its symptoms look like other common conditions or like the normal changes of menopause. When a computer model tries to predict how a patient's symptoms will evolve, it can be fooled into blaming Long COVID for what is really background physiology. We built a model based on a small language model that reads a written summary of each patient-their history, comorbidities, and a month of wearable-device data-and is explicitly trained to separate "true disease signal" from "background noise." We tested it against standard predictors at 3, 6, and 9 months. We report an finding that is easy to overlook: because Long COVID severity changes slowly, simply assuming a patient's next score equals their last score is very accurate and hard to beat for stable patients. Our model's advantage appears where it matters clinically-patients whose symptoms are actually changing-and, importantly, the model shows which words drove its prediction , correctly emphasizing symptoms like breathlessness while down-weighting confounders like menopause. We argue this interpretability, not a small accuracy gain, is the real contribution.

papers.title: Whole person health across sociodemographic groups of adults in the United States.
papers.abstract: Chronic disease accounts for most health care expenditures in the United States (US), highlighting the need for approaches that address health across interconnected spiritual, mental/emotional, behavioral, physical (including environmental), and social domains. Whole person health (WPH) is increasingly recognized as important for alleviating chronic disease burdens but has not been well-described across various sociodemographic groups of US adults. Using cross-sectional data from the 2025 National Health Interview Survey, we sought to describe the prevalence of WPH and its components among US adults overall and by age, sex, and race along with ethnicity. Participants responded to the nine-item Whole Person Health Index (WPHI), which we used to assess continuous scores (range: 9-45, where higher scores indicated improved health) and "optimal" (excellent/very good vs. good/fair/poor) overall and domain-specific WPH. Using survey procedures, we estimated medians (IQR) and prevalence (95% CI) and compared subgroups using multiple comparison correction. Among 23,884 NHIS participants aged 18 years and older (mean age (SE)=48 (0.2) years), representing approximately 261,620,640 US adults, the median WPHI score was 33 (28-37) and slightly over half (57% [56%-58%]) of adults were classified as having " optimal " overall WPH. Optimal social/family connections (72% [72%-73%]) were frequently reported; " optimal " sleep was infrequently reported (36% [35%-37%]). WPH and its components were generally highest among younger adults. Men and women differed in WPH domains but not in overall WPH. Non-Hispanic (NH) American Indian/Native Alaskan and NH-Black adults generally had lowest prevalence of optimal WPH and its components, which was often higher among Hispanic/Latino adults and highest among NH-Asian and White adults. These results showing variation in WPH in the US may inform future investigations of WPH, related predictors and health outcomes, and health disparities.

papers.title: A Nationally Representative Study of Complementary and Alternative Medicine Therapies in relation to Sleep Duration and Insomnia Symptoms among US Adults.
papers.abstract: Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) therapies, such as massage, meditation, and yoga, are widely used to promote wellness, including sleep improvement. Although some CAM therapies may improve sleep through stress reduction, relaxation, and relief of physical discomfort, little is known about associations between individual CAM modalities and sleep health at the population level. Therefore, we investigated the associations between CAM therapies and short sleep duration as well as insomnia symptoms. Participants from the nationally-representative 2012 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) self-reported the use of CAM therapies and short sleep duration (<7 hours vs. 7-9 hours) as well as insomnia symptoms (yes vs. no). Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for cross-sectional associations between CAM therapy use and sleep outcomes. Among 30,405 participants, the average age was 46.1 ± 0.2 years and 51% were women. Adults reporting any vs. no CAM therapy use had a higher prevalence of short sleep duration (aPR: 1.11; 95% CI: 1.05-1.16) and insomnia symptoms (aPR: 1.56; 95% CI: 1.47- 1.65) after adjustment for sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. Herbal supplements (aPR: 1.13; 95% CI: 1.07-1.19) and massage (aPR: 1.14; 95% CI: 1.05-1.23) were associated with higher prevalence of short sleep duration. Most CAM therapies were associated with higher prevalence of insomnia symptoms, with the strongest associations observed for meditation/guided imagery/progressive relaxation (aPR: 1.84; 95% CI: 1.68-2.02). The higher prevalence of short sleep duration and insomnia symptoms among CAM users may reflect reverse causation, as adults with more severe or persistent sleep disturbances may be more likely to seek CAM therapies. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify directionality.

papers.title: Label-Free Live Cell Type Prediction by Integrating Raman Spectroscopy and Machine Learning.
papers.abstract: Coherent Raman spectroscopy enables label-free biochemical fingerprinting of live cells with subcellular resolution. We previously developed a machine learning framework capable of classifying glioma FFPE tissues using Raman spectral signatures. To accelerate live cell acquisition, we previously developed RADAR (Raman Spectral Analysis Using Deep Learning for Artifact Removal), a method that increases imaging speed by an order of magnitude while preserving spectral integrity. By integrating high-speed Raman imaging with supervised machine learning, we aimed to define unique biochemical fingerprints specific to cell type. We hypothesized that intrinsic biochemical composition alone is sufficient to distinguish cellular identity and tumor subtype. To test this, we generated metabolic maps of diverse brain-derived cell types-including astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, and glioblastoma cells-using coherent Raman spectroscopy at single-cell resolution. Patient-derived brain tumor cell lines representing genetically heterogeneous backgrounds were analyzed. Samples were stratified by IDH1 mutation status (IDH1-mutant and IDH1-wild-type) and histologically classified as oligodendroglioma or astrocytoma. Raman spectral data were acquired from 286 live single cells across the two principal molecular classes, with further subdivision into two histologic subtypes within the IDH1-mutant group. Classification was performed using an XGBoost model with shallow tree depth (1-3), a 20% held-out test set, and grouped, stratified 5-fold cross-validation to control for sample-level bias. The machine learning framework distinguished IDH1-mutant from IDH1-wild-type cells with a ROC-AUC of 0.78 and further discriminated IDH1-mutant astrocytoma from oligodendroglioma cells with a ROC-AUC of 0.81. Feature importance analysis demonstrated that separation between IDH1-mutant and IDH1-wild-type cells was driven primarily by Raman peaks associated with protein amide bands, total NADH, unsaturated fatty acids, and heme-related vibrational modes. Within the IDH1-mutant class, discrimination between oligodendroglioma and astrocytoma was driven by lipid-rich vesicle signatures, protein/polyamide amide bands, and lipid-associated spectral features. Together, these findings support the feasibility of label-free, machine learning-assisted Raman profiling to resolve clinically relevant glioma subtypes at single-cell resolution. This scalable analytical framework provides a translational platform for investigating metabolic heterogeneity, therapeutic response, co-culture systems, and patient-derived organoid models.
